senses.example: Her small bakery began to blossom after the magazine featured her cakes.

core.definition: A flower, especially one on a tree or shrub that will develop into fruit, or the mass of such flowers.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, not a strong sum vowel. The first vowel is the open ah of American cot and caught.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests beauty, new life, promise, and growth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use blossom for flowers on fruit trees such as apple, cherry, and peach, as in 'the cherry blossoms are out in D.C.' For flowers in general, people more often say 'flowers' or 'blooms'. As a verb, 'bloom' is more common for plants, while 'blossom' is used for people or projects that flourish, as in 'she really blossomed in college'.

distinctions.note: Bloom is the broader word for any flowering plant and the open state of flowers, while blossom is typically used for tree and shrub flowers.
Flower is the general term for the reproductive part of a plant, and it is also used for a single bloom in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: The cherry blossoms are already out, so let's take the kids down to the park this weekend.
examples.professional: The new hire really blossomed once she took ownership of the data pipeline, so we promoted her last quarter.
examples.analytical: Many poets link the blossom to hope because it appears before the fruit, so the promise matters even when the harvest is uncertain.

nuance.analogy: Like a promising start before the harvest: the blossom shows what is coming, though it does not yet bear fruit.
nuance.etymology: From Old English blostma, related to bloom, both from a common Germanic root.
common_mistakes: Using blossom for every flower; it is mainly for trees and shrubs, while flower or bloom is more general.
Pronouncing the first vowel as a long o, as in 'BLOH-sum'; American speech uses the open ah sound.
Using blossoms as a plural for a single flower; one flower is 'a blossom'.
nuance.biblical_note: Blossom appears in Scripture as a sign of renewal, fruitfulness, and divine blessing. Numbers 17:8 describes Aaron's rod producing blossoms and almonds, a sign that God chose Aaron's line, using the Hebrew perach. Isaiah 35:1-2 promises that the desert will blossom as the crocus. James 1:10-11 uses the flower of the grass as an image of how quickly human wealth fades.

senses.definition: The quality or characteristic of being blue in color.
Melancholy.

core.definition: The quality of being blue in color; in literary use it can also suggest a state of sadness or melancholy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BLOO, and the final -ness is a reduced schwa, so say 'nus' rather than 'nes'. Keep the first vowel long, as in 'blue'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing color; poetic and slightly melancholy in literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use blueness in everyday talk. They would say 'the blue of the sky' or 'how blue it is' instead. The word appears in descriptions of skies, water and paint, and in literature. The sense of sadness is archaic and you will seldom hear it today.

distinctions.note: Blue is the everyday word for the color itself, while blueness is the abstract noun for the quality, used mostly in writing.
Blueness means the full quality of being blue, while bluishness suggests only a slight blue tint.

examples.everyday: Look at the blueness of that lake, it looks like a postcard.
examples.professional: The paint sample's blueness looked too cold under the office lights, so we chose a warmer shade.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of perception have long asked whether the blueness we see in the sky belongs to the sky or to our visual experience.

nuance.analogy: Blueness is to blue as sweetness is to sugar: it names the quality itself, apart from the thing that has it.
nuance.etymology: From blue (Old English blǣw) plus the suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of being blue.
common_mistakes: Using blueness for the color in everyday speech; say 'blue' or 'the blue' instead.
Pronouncing the final -ness with a full vowel; it is a reduced schwa, 'nus'.

senses.definition: Wholeheartedly.

core.definition: Completely and with total commitment, using all of one's energy; also the whole human person as physical and spiritual.

pronunciation.tip: Body has a flapped d, sounding like BAH-dee. In speech, "and" reduces to 'n or und, so it sounds like BAH-dee-un-SOHL. The l in soul is clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests wholehearted devotion. In theology, it expresses the unity of the human person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say "threw himself into it body and soul" or "gave it everything." It is a bit literary but understood by everyone. In theology it highlights that humans are bodily and spiritual together, not souls in bodies.

distinctions.note: Heart and soul stresses emotion and passion; body and soul adds the sense of the whole self, including physical effort.
Wholeheartedly is a single adverb and emphasizes sincerity, not total physical and spiritual commitment.
This longer phrase lists three aspects of a person and is common in wellness talk.

collocations: throw oneself into it body and soul

examples.everyday: She threw herself into the garden body and soul, and now it looks amazing.
examples.professional: Our founder gave this company body and soul for twenty years before retiring.
examples.analytical: Christian anthropology insists that the human being is body and soul together, so salvation must include the resurrection of the body.

nuance.analogy: Like rowing with every muscle and every bit of your will, nothing held back.
nuance.etymology: A phrase from Middle English, joining body and soul as the two parts of a person.
common_mistakes: Saying "with body and soul" instead of "body and soul."
Pronouncing body with a hard d instead of a flap.
Confusing it with "keep body and soul together," which means to survive financially.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture treats the person as a unity. Genesis 2:7 says God formed man from dust and breathed life into him so he became a living being. In Matthew 10:28, Jesus speaks of God who can destroy both soul and body in hell. 1 Thessalonians 5:23 prays that spirit, soul, and body be kept sound.

senses.definition: A rumbling sound made by the movement of gas in the intestines.
Something resembling borborygmus.

core.definition: The rumbling or gurgling noise made by gas moving through the intestines, often heard as a stomach growl.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, RIG, with weaker stress on the first syllable. The final -mus is unstressed, and the g is hard, as in 'big.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It can sound playful or pretentious in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors and writers use borborygmus, while everyday Americans say stomach growling or tummy rumbling. Using the word at a dinner table can sound showy unless you are joking or talking with a medical professional. It describes a normal sound and is not serious by itself.

distinctions.note: Flatulence means passing gas; borborygmus is the rumbling sound of gas moving through the intestines, which may happen without passing gas.
A stomach growl is the everyday phrase for a hunger noise; borborygmus is the clinical term for any intestinal rumble.

examples.everyday: My stomach gave this huge borborygmus in the middle of the movie, and everyone turned around.
examples.professional: The nurse noted active borborygmus on the exam, which suggested the bowel sounds were normal.
examples.analytical: Borborygmus is a sound without a clear meaning, yet writers have used it to convey hunger and bodily vulnerability.

nuance.analogy: Like a radiator knocking and gurgling as steam moves through the pipes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek borborygmos, an imitative word for a rumbling sound.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in bor-BOR-ygmus; the main stress is on RIG.
Pronouncing the g as a soft j sound; it is hard, as in 'big.'

borborygmus.etymology: From New Latin *borborygmus*, from Ancient Greek *βορβορυγμός*, of origin.

senses.definition: A person or thing that bounces something, such as a ball.
senses.example: The toy company's new bouncer launches foam balls across the playground for toddlers.

senses.definition: A member of security personnel employed by bars, nightclubs, etc. to decide who can enter, maintain order, and deal with patrons who cause trouble.
senses.example: The bouncer at the downtown club checked our IDs before letting us inside.

senses.definition: An account or server (as with IRC and FTP) that invisibly redirects requests to another, used for anonymity or vanity.
senses.example: To hide his location, he routed all his traffic through a bouncer on a remote server.

senses.definition: Something big; a good stout example of the kind.
senses.example: That 12-pound trout was a real bouncer, the biggest fish we caught all summer.

senses.definition: A bouncy castle.
senses.example: The kids spent the whole birthday party jumping in the bouncer on our front lawn.

senses.definition: A kind of seat mounted in a framework in which a baby can bounce up and down.
senses.example: We set the baby in the bouncer so I could finally finish washing the dishes.

senses.definition: Short for shop-bouncer.
senses.example: The store installed a bouncer by the exit to stop shoplifters from leaving.

senses.definition: A short-pitched ball that bounces up towards, or above the height of the batsman’s head.
senses.example: The bowler sent a vicious bouncer that flew past the batsman's helmet.

senses.definition: (dated) One who bounces; a large, heavy person who makes much noise in moving.
senses.example: That big bouncer of a farmhand stomped across the porch and rattled every window.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A security worker at a bar or nightclub who decides who may enter, keeps order, and removes troublemakers.

pronunciation.tip: The word has two syllables, with stress on the first. The final -er is a reduced rhotic vowel, so say it as a soft 'sur,' not 'sir' or 'ur-ray.' Do not split it into bounce-er with a long vowel in the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes a job that can sound intimidating, but it is not an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say bouncer for the person at the door of a bar, club, or party who checks IDs and handles drunk or aggressive guests. A hotel doorman or building doorman is a different job, so do not use bouncer for them. At a bar, you might say 'The bouncer checked my ID,' and a polite reply is simply 'Thanks' or 'Sure, here you go.'

distinctions.note: A doorman in the US usually works at a hotel or apartment building and greets guests. A bouncer works at a bar or club and enforces entry rules and order.
A security guard protects a building or property in general. A bouncer is specialized for nightlife venues and entry control.

examples.everyday: The bouncer at the bar asked for our IDs before letting us in.
examples.professional: We hired two extra bouncers for the company party so the check-in line would move faster.
examples.analytical: The bouncer's authority is a delegated form of social control, and its limits depend on the rules of the venue rather than on law alone.

nuance.analogy: A bouncer is like a gatekeeper at a castle, deciding who gets through the door and who must leave.
nuance.etymology: From bounce (to throw out or force out, in the sense of expelling someone) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the word as BOWN-sir or with a long e sound at the end.
Using bouncer for a hotel or apartment doorman, which Americans would call a doorman.

senses.definition: To enter a place by force or illicit means.
senses.example: Someone broke in and stole his radio.

senses.definition: To interrupt one's conversation; speak before another person has finished speaking.
senses.example: Please don't break in while I'm talking; let me finish my point first.

senses.definition: To reach a state of functioning more smoothly through use or wear; to cause (something, or someone, new) to undergo this change.
senses.example: These shoes will be more comfortable after they have broken in.

senses.definition: To tame; make obedient; to train to follow orders of the owner.
senses.example: The rancher spent the summer trying to break in a wild mustang for his daughter.

senses.definition: To smash (something) by forcing it inward.
senses.example: A falling branch broke in the rear window of our car during the storm.

senses.definition: Starting something brand new or at a new level.
senses.example: He broke in with the New York Yankees.

senses.definition: To take the virginity of a girl, to deflower.
senses.example: The rake boasted in the tavern that he meant to break in the innocent farmer's daughter before spring.

senses.definition: To initiate a new person into prostitution or prison sex acts.
senses.example: The older inmates warned the new arrival that the gang would break in anyone who came in weak.

core.definition: To enter a building or vehicle by force or illegally, or to make new shoes or equipment comfortable through use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on in, the particle, in American speech. The vowel in in is short, so keep it brief and do not stretch it into 'een'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it means illegal entry, and neutral when it means making shoes or equipment comfortable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say someone broke in to my house last night to describe a burglary; the police will ask if the door was broken in or forced open. For shoes, people say I'm breaking in these new boots. In sports or business, break in can also mean to train a new person, as in breaking in a new hire.

distinctions.note: Break in is often used without an object, while break into requires an object, as in broke into the car.
Burglarize is a formal or legal word for stealing from a building, while break in describes the act of forcing entry, which may or may not involve theft.

examples.everyday: Somebody broke in to our garage and took the bikes, so we installed a new lock.
examples.professional: We need to break in the new analysts gradually, pairing them with senior staff for their first month.
examples.analytical: In this argument, the state tries to break in on private life, which raises questions about the limits of authority.

nuance.analogy: Breaking in new shoes is like taming a horse: at first it is stiff and uncomfortable, but with use it fits the rider.
nuance.etymology: From Old English brecan, to break, plus in, indicating entry into a place.
common_mistakes: Saying break in the house without into; say break into the house.
Using break in as a noun in the same way as the phrasal verb; use break-in for the noun.

conversation.text: Someone broke in last night and stole our TV.
I need to break in these new boots before the hike.
Sorry to break in, but your Uber is here.
We're still breaking in the new guy at work.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, resembling, or containing brine (“water saturated or strongly impregnated with salt”), such as seawater or tears; salty.
senses.example: on the briny deep

senses.definition: Of a person: difficult to get along with or to like; acerbic, prickly, unlikable.
senses.example: Nobody wanted to sit next to the briny old neighbor at the block party.

senses.definition: The ocean, the sea.
senses.example: The fishermen headed back out to the briny before the storm rolled in.

core.definition: Containing or tasting of salt, like seawater; salty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-y' is a clear 'ee' sound, not 'ay,' so 'briny' is 'BRY-nee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in descriptive writing. It evokes the sea, fresh seafood, or sharp salty air, but it can sound poetic in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'briny' mainly when describing the sea, oysters, pickle brine, or sea air, often in food writing or travel description. In casual conversation 'salty' is more common. The noun sense 'the sea' is old and poetic, so avoid it in ordinary speech.

distinctions.note: 'Salty' is everyday and general, while 'briny' is more literary and specifically suggests seawater or brine.
'Saline' is technical, used in chemistry, medicine, and biology for salt solutions, and does not usually describe a pleasant taste or sea air.
'Brackish' describes water that is partly salty, a mix of fresh and salt water, often in estuaries or marshes; 'briny' describes strongly salty water.

examples.everyday: I love the briny smell of the ocean when we get to the beach in the morning.
examples.professional: The lab's briny water samples have to be filtered before we run the salinity test.
examples.analytical: Melville's briny imagery links the sea with both danger and renewal throughout the novel.

nuance.analogy: Like a pickle jar's liquid: a briny taste that clearly comes from the sea of salt.
nuance.etymology: From 'brine' (salt water), from Old English brȳne, plus the suffix '-y.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final '-y' as 'ay' ('BRY-nay') instead of 'ee.'
Using 'briny' as an everyday word for any salty food, when Americans usually say 'salty' for snacks or soup.
Using the noun sense 'the briny' for the sea in casual speech, which sounds old-fashioned.

senses.definition: The state of being brutal.
A cruel or savage act.
The use of excessive physical force, often in the form of violence.
senses.example: police brutality

core.definition: Extreme cruelty or violence, or the act of acting in an excessively harsh or violent way toward others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves to the middle syllable, 'TAL', unlike the adjective 'BROO-tuhl'. The vowel in 'tal' is the flat 'a' of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes shocking violence or cruelty and is serious in tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use brutality in serious news, legal, political, and human-rights contexts, such as 'police brutality' or 'the brutality of war'. In casual conversation, it is strong and should be reserved for real violence or cruelty. For milder cases, people often say 'harsh treatment' or 'mistreatment'.

distinctions.note: Cruelty is a broad word for deliberate harm; brutality stresses physical violence that is extreme or shocking.
Violence is the general use of force; brutality adds a sense of excessive, savage cruelty beyond what is necessary.

examples.everyday: I can't watch the news lately because the brutality in those videos is too much.
examples.professional: The investigation found no physical brutality, but the manager's public humiliation of staff was inappropriate.
examples.analytical: The ambiguity between state violence and legal order makes brutality a central problem for political theology, since the state claims to restrain the very violence it sometimes uses.

nuance.analogy: Brutality is the raw, unfiltered version of cruelty: cruelty can be quiet, but brutality is loud, physical, and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From French brutalité, from Latin brutalis, 'of an animal or without reason'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on 'bru': say broo-TAL-uh-tee.
Using brutality for a single harsh remark; say 'harsh' or 'unkind' instead for milder situations.

senses.definition: Without reason or intelligence (of animals).
senses.example: a brute beast

senses.definition: Characteristic of unthinking animals; senseless, unreasoning (of humans).
senses.example: Brute instinct drove the crowd to push toward the exits without a thought.

senses.definition: Unconnected with intelligence or thought; purely material, senseless.
senses.example: the brute earth; the brute powers of nature

senses.definition: Crude, unpolished.
Strong, blunt, and spontaneous; being purely physical in nature.
senses.example: I got the door open through brute force.

senses.definition: Brutal; cruel; fierce; ferocious; savage; pitiless, without intelligence or reason.
senses.example: brute violence

senses.definition: A person with the characteristics of an unthinking animal; a coarse or brutal person, particularly one who is dim-witted.
senses.example: One of them was a hulking brute of a man, heavily tattooed and with a hardened face that practically screamed "I just got out of jail."

senses.definition: A kind of powerful spotlight.
senses.example: The stage crew rolled in a brute to light the singer's solo during the final song.

senses.definition: To shape (diamonds) by grinding them against each other.
senses.example: The cutter spent three days bruting the rough stone before polishing its facets.

core.definition: Using raw physical strength rather than skill, thought, or subtlety; crude and forceful, as in 'brute force.'

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'oo' vowel and a clear American r before the vowel, so say 'broot' with no y-glide. Do not shorten it to 'but' or stretch it to 'brew-t.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests crudeness, lack of finesse, or cruelty, and is sometimes used neutrally for raw force in technical contexts like 'brute-force attack.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'brute' in the phrase 'brute force,' meaning force used without strategy, such as breaking down a door or trying every password. As a noun, 'a brute' is a harsh insult for a violent or insensitive person and sounds strong and somewhat old-fashioned. In casual talk, you will mostly hear the adjective in fixed phrases.

distinctions.note: Brutal describes cruelty or savagery or something harsh and painful, such as a brutal winter; brute describes raw force or a creature-like lack of refinement, such as brute strength.
Brutish means like a beast, crude, or stupid in manner, and is almost always an insult; brute is more neutral when describing force, as in brute force.
Sheer emphasizes complete degree, as in sheer luck; brute emphasizes unthinking, physical power, as in brute strength.

examples.everyday: My brother just used brute force to pull the stuck lid off the jar.
examples.professional: Our security team flagged a brute-force attack, where the script tried thousands of passwords per minute.
examples.analytical: Kant would say that a merely brute-force moral rule, obeyed out of fear, lacks the autonomy that makes an act good.

nuance.analogy: Brute force is like a sledgehammer, while a skilled approach is like a precision screwdriver: both can open the lock, but only one is elegant.
nuance.etymology: From Latin brutus, meaning heavy, dull, or senseless.
common_mistakes: Using 'brute' for cruelty where 'brutal' is correct, as in 'a brute winter' instead of 'a brutal winter.'
Saying the vowel as in 'but' instead of the long 'oo' in 'brute.'
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the Greek alogos, meaning unreasoning or without reason, for animals that act by instinct. In 2 Peter 2:12 (RSV), false teachers are compared to irrational animals, creatures of instinct, destined to be caught and destroyed. Psalm 49:20 (RSV) says that a person who has honor but lacks understanding is like the beasts that perish, showing that human beings are called to reason and wisdom.

brute.etymology: From Middle French *brut*, from Old French *brut*, from Latin *brūtus* (“dull, stupid, insensible”), an loanword, from Proto-Indo-European **gʷréh₂us* (“heavy”).

senses.definition: A light blow or jolting collision.
senses.example: His car had a tiny bump with a moving bus.

senses.definition: The sound of such a collision.
senses.example: He heard a loud bump and saw the front part of his car was broken and the driver of the other car was running to apologize.

senses.definition: Any light sound.
senses.example: He heard bumps in the night.

senses.definition: A fist bump.
senses.example: I held my fist up, and he gave me a bump before leaving.

senses.definition: A car accident, usually a small one.
senses.example: I had a bump last time I drove into the city.

senses.definition: A collision, especially a fall.
senses.example: Did you see the bump he took last night?

senses.definition: A dose of a drug, such as ketamine or cocaine, snorted; a small dose of a snorted drug.
senses.example: He admitted he had taken a bump of cocaine before the party ended.

senses.definition: A conflict.
senses.example: The bump between the two neighbors over the fence lasted for months.

senses.definition: A protuberance on a flat surface or a straight line.
senses.example: Be careful of that bump in the road.

senses.definition: A swelling on the skin caused by illness or injury.
senses.example: A bump rose on her forehead after she hit the cabinet door.

senses.definition: A bouffant hairstyle; the puffy upper part of such a hairstyle.
senses.example: She looks great with that bump Kelly gave her at the salon.

senses.definition: The swollen abdomen of a pregnant woman.
senses.example: The midwife said her bump looked healthy at thirty-two weeks.

senses.definition: A small increase in an amount.
senses.example: His pay got a bump last month.

senses.definition: A small increase in excitement or interest.
senses.example: The addition of the fight scenes gave the story a little bump near the end, but overall, it bored me.

senses.definition: A temporary, usually small, increase in a quantity, such as is shown in a graph.
senses.example: US presidential nominees get a post-convention bump in survey ratings.

senses.definition: A ripoff or bad deal; an unjustly high price.
senses.example: I paid a hundred pounds for that, but it was a proper bump, mate.

senses.definition: A minor problem or difficulty.
senses.example: Finding parking downtown was a minor bump in an otherwise smooth day.

senses.definition: Senses related to a movement, especially a rhythmic or sudden one.
senses.example: The fetus can hear the bump of the mother's heartbeat.

senses.definition: The point, in a race in which boats are spaced apart at the start, at which a boat begins to overtake the boat ahead.
senses.example: The coxswain called for the bump as our boat closed on the lead.

senses.definition: The act of using one's forearm to strike the ball in a volleyball match.
senses.example: She went up for a bump to keep the ball alive in the rally.

senses.definition: In skipping, a single jump over two consecutive turns of the rope.
senses.example: In speed skipping, she practiced a bump over two turns of the rope.

senses.definition: A sudden movement of underground strata, preceded by a characteristic sound.
senses.example: Miners reported a sudden bump in the coal seam before the rock shifted.

senses.definition: A post in an Internet forum thread made in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.
senses.example: He posted a bump to the forum thread to push it back to the top.

senses.definition: In the game of khanhoo, the act of claiming a newly discarded card when it is not one's turn, permitted when one can use the card to form a meld other than a sequence.
senses.example: In khanhoo, she bumped the discard out of turn to complete a meld.

senses.definition: A good song, especially a danceable one.
senses.example: His latest song is such a bump, I can't stop listening to it on repeat.

senses.definition: A reassignment of jobs within an organization (for example, when an existing employee leaves) on the basis of seniority.
senses.example: When the supervisor retired, a bump moved two seniors into new roles.

senses.definition: A demotion or promotion.
senses.example: He got a bump up into senior management.

senses.definition: A coarse cotton fabric.
senses.example: Her grandmother sewed aprons from sturdy bump cotton bought at the market.

senses.definition: A training match for a fighting dog.
senses.example: The breeder scheduled a bump for his terrier before the regional championship.

senses.definition: The jaw of either of the middle pockets.
senses.example: The cue ball struck the bump of the side pocket and spun away.

senses.definition: A short, self-promotional spot on a radio or television station.
senses.example: The station aired a quick bump promoting the morning show.

senses.definition: The breeding call made by the bittern; a boom.
The sound and other sensations of a rhythm, especially in music with a strong, danceable beat, especially played over speakers at loud volume with strong bass frequency response.
senses.example: The fetus can hear the bump of the mother's heartbeat.

senses.definition: A disco dance in which partners rhythmically bump their hips together.
senses.example: I saw him doing The Bump with her.

senses.definition: An undercover contact or staged encounter used to elicit information, prompt a reaction, or arrange a follow-up meeting with a suspect or person of interest.
(dated) The faculty itself.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To knock against or run into with a jolt.
senses.example: Their car got bumped while they were turning at the junction.

senses.definition: To move up or down by a step; displace.
senses.example: I bumped the font size up to make my document easier to read.

senses.definition: To post in an Internet forum thread in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.
To move (a booked passenger) to a later flight because of earlier delays or cancellations.
To move the time of (a scheduled event).
To pick (a lock) with a repeated striking motion that dislodges the pins.
To increase (a version number).
To assassinate; to bump off.
To displace (another employee in an organization) on the basis of seniority.
In the game of khanhoo, to claim a newly discarded card when it is not one's turn, permitted when one can use the card to form a meld other than a sequence.
To play music through a speaker, often loudly and in public.
To move while bumping up and down, as a cart or car does on rough ground.
senses.example: The car bumped over the dirt road.

senses.definition: To snort a small dose of cocaine or another drug; to do a bump of a drug.
senses.example: She bumped some of that coke off her house key.

senses.definition: To evade fare collection in public transport.
senses.example: If you can bump Dartford Station, you can get into Buckingham Palace.

senses.definition: Of a bittern, to make its characteristic breeding call.
To suddenly boil, causing movement of the vessel and loss of liquid.
To encounter and stop, to catch.
(dated) To anger, irritate.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To spread out material so as to fill any desired number of pages.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Posted in an Internet forum thread in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.

core.definition: A light blow or jolting collision, such as hitting your head on a low cabinet or a car hitting a speed bump.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the only syllable. End the word with the lips closed for the p, and do not add a vowel after it; the final -mp cluster is one quick sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. A bump can be minor or painful, and the context shows which.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bump for a minor accident or knock, as in 'I got a bump on my head,' and for a small rise, as in 'a bump in sales.' You can also say 'bump into someone' for meeting them by chance. Phrases like 'bump up the price' are common in business, and 'bumps' can mean a rough stretch of road or a difficult patch in life.

distinctions.note: A knock usually means a deliberate tap or a hit on a surface, while a bump is an accidental jolt or collision.
A jolt is a sudden shaking movement, often from a vehicle, while a bump is a specific impact with something.
A bruise is the injury that may follow a bump, so a bump is the cause and a bruise is the result.

examples.everyday: Watch out, you'll bump your head on that low beam.
examples.professional: The new model gave us a small bump in accuracy, about one percent.
examples.analytical: A single bump in the loss curve can look like a bug, but it often reflects the learning-rate schedule.

nuance.analogy: Like a car rolling over a speed bump: a short, sudden jolt before the road goes on as before.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of a dull, heavy knock.
common_mistakes: Adding a vowel after the final p, as 'BUMP-uh', which makes it sound like a different word.
Using 'bump' for a serious crash; it suggests a minor impact, so say 'accident' or 'crash' for serious events.
Confusing 'bump into' (meet by chance) with 'bump into' (hit physically) without context.

bump.etymology: probably of origin; compare, all probably of origin.

senses.definition: Methodical and efficient, in a way that would be advantageous to a business or businessperson.
senses.example: She handled the negotiation in a calm, businesslike manner that impressed the investors.

senses.definition: Earnest and practical without being distracted or enthusiastic.

core.definition: Efficient, serious, and practical, without unnecessary chatter, emotion, or distraction, as suited to work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BIZ. The middle syllable is a short, reduced vowel, so say 'BIZ-nis', not 'BIZ-nes' with a clear e, and 'like' is one long syllable.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, suggesting competence and focus. It can sound cold if used of someone who seems unfriendly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'businesslike' to praise a calm, organized manner, as in 'She ran the meeting in a businesslike way.' It is often used to describe emails, tone, or meetings. In writing, Americans usually write it as one word, without a hyphen.

distinctions.note: Professional is broader and covers skill, ethics, and conduct, while businesslike focuses on a no-nonsense, efficient manner.
Formal refers to rules, dress, and etiquette, and can be cold; businesslike suggests practical efficiency more than ceremony.
Efficient describes results or use of resources; businesslike describes a way of behaving in a business setting.

examples.everyday: My landlord was very businesslike on the phone, so I just gave him the rent details and hung up.
examples.professional: Keep your emails businesslike: state the decision, list the next steps, and skip the small talk.
examples.analytical: Weber's account of bureaucracy describes a businesslike impersonality that values rules over personal relationships.

nuance.analogy: A businesslike meeting is like a well-run sprint review: an agenda, clear decisions, and no wasted minutes.
nuance.etymology: Business plus -like, meaning 'resembling' or 'in the manner of.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'business-like' with a hyphen; most American writers use one word.
Using 'businesslike' as a noun, as in 'He is a businesslike'; it is an adjective describing manner.

senses.definition: P-code (various forms of instruction sets designed for efficient execution by a software interpreter as well as being suitable for further compilation into machine code).
senses.example: The Java compiler converts source code into bytecode that the virtual machine can run on any platform.

core.definition: Compact low-level instructions produced by compiling source code, which a virtual machine or interpreter executes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, BYTE, and the final syllable is 'code' with a long o. Do not pronounce the t in byte as a hard stop before the k; it is a clear t followed by a k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used precisely by programmers.
nuance.usage_note: American developers use this word in discussions of Java, Python and .NET, and in compiler or runtime design reviews. It is not a term for everyday conversation. A natural reply in a code review is 'Did you check the bytecode output?'

distinctions.note: Machine code runs directly on hardware, while bytecode is an intermediate format executed by a virtual machine or interpreter.
Source code is written by humans in a programming language, whereas bytecode is generated from it and is not meant for people to read.

examples.everyday: My brother works on a game engine, and he says the scripts get turned into bytecode before they run.
examples.professional: The build step compiles the service to bytecode, so the same artifact runs on any JVM.
examples.analytical: Bytecode occupies a middle layer: it is portable like source code yet efficient like machine code.

nuance.analogy: Like sheet music that a band can play on any instrument: the music is written once, then each machine plays it its own way.
nuance.etymology: Bytecode combines byte, a unit of eight bits, and code, a set of instructions; the term dates from the 1960s.
common_mistakes: Assuming bytecode is human-readable like source code.
Confusing bytecode with machine code, which the processor runs directly.

senses.definition: A compartment at the front of a truck or train for the driver.
senses.example: The truck driver rested his coffee on the dashboard inside the cab during the long night shift.

senses.definition: A similar compartment in other vehicles.
senses.example: We climbed into the cab of the rented van, and the seats smelled faintly of pine air freshener.

senses.definition: A shelter at the top of an air traffic control tower or fire lookout tower.
senses.example: The controller in the cab atop the tower watched the runway lights blink through the fog.

senses.definition: Synonym of taxi, a vehicle available for public hire for single journeys.
senses.example: a cab ride

senses.definition: An arcade cabinet, the unit in which a video game is housed in a gaming arcade.
senses.example: My brother spent every Saturday feeding quarters into a racing game cab at the mall arcade.

senses.definition: Clipping of cabinet file (“a compressed library archive file”).
senses.example: Before uploading, I packed the project files into a single cab so the install would be faster.

senses.definition: Short for cabernet sauvignon.
senses.example: We ordered a bottle of cab from Napa to go with the grilled lamb.

senses.definition: (historical) Any of several two- or four-wheeled carriages; a cabriolet.
senses.example: In the 1890s, a wealthy merchant rode through town in a two-wheeled cab pulled by a single horse.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A former Hebrew unit of volume, about equal to 1.3 L as a dry measure or 1.25 L as a liquid measure.
senses.example: The ancient scribe measured the grain carefully, filling a cab with barley for each family's share.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To travel by taxicab.
senses.example: We were so tired after the concert that we decided to cab it back to the hotel.

core.definition: A taxi, which is a car with a driver that carries passengers for a fare.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a as in 'cat' and end with a clear, unvoiced b sound. Do not confuse it with 'cap', which ends with a p sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cab informally to mean taxi, especially in New York, Chicago and other big cities. You might hear 'Grab a cab' or 'Let's take a cab.' In airports and hotels, people often say taxi, but the meaning is the same. A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll call one.'

distinctions.note: Taxi is the standard word everywhere, while cab is the more informal American term that is especially common in big cities.
A rideshare is booked through an app with a private driver, while a cab is a licensed taxi that you hail or call for.

examples.everyday: It's raining hard, so let's grab a cab instead of walking to the restaurant.
examples.professional: I'll take a cab from the airport to the client's office, so expense it under travel.
examples.analytical: The cab, as a regulated form of transport, reflects a longstanding urban compromise between access and control.

nuance.analogy: Like a short cut to a destination: instead of walking, you take the quick ride that someone else drives.
nuance.etymology: Short for cabriolet, a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage, from French cabriolet.
common_mistakes: Using cab to mean the front compartment of a truck, which is a different sense.
Saying 'a cab' when you mean the service; say 'by cab' or 'take a cab' instead.

conversation.text: Let's grab a cab; it's too far to walk.
I hailed a cab outside the hotel.
The cab line at the airport was really long.

senses.definition: Displaying the properties of bad spelling or bad handwriting or both.
senses.example: The cacographic draft was full of misspelled words and illegible scrawl.

core.definition: Showing bad spelling or bad handwriting.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on GRAF, with a lighter secondary stress on 'KAK'. The vowel in the middle 'uh' is reduced, so do not say each syllable equally.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes writing or spelling that is clearly poor, often in a critical or humorous way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cacographic' mostly in scholarly or literary writing, such as discussions of manuscripts, editing or historical letters. In ordinary speech, people say 'sloppy' or 'badly spelled' instead. It sounds stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Illegible means impossible to read, while cacographic describes spelling or writing that is poor in quality, even if readable.
Sloppy is informal and general, while cacographic is precise and academic, focusing on spelling and handwriting.
Misspelled refers to a particular word, while cacographic describes a whole body of poor writing.

examples.everyday: My mom's shopping lists are so cacographic that I can never tell whether she wrote milk or silk.
examples.professional: The client's draft contains so many cacographic errors that we need to proofread it before sending it to legal.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the cacographic spelling in these medieval letters reflects the scribe's education or his haste.

nuance.analogy: A cacographic page is like a road full of potholes: you can still travel it, but every step is bumpy.
nuance.etymology: From cacography, from Greek kakos, 'bad', and graphein, 'to write'.
common_mistakes: Using 'cacographic' for spoken errors; it refers to writing and spelling.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'kak-uh-GRAF-ick'.

senses.definition: A frame or framework.
senses.example: A wooden cadre supports the clay mold until the sculpture hardens.

senses.definition: The core of a managing group, or a member of such a group.
senses.example: She joined the company's leadership cadre after ten years of managing projects.

senses.definition: A small group of people specially trained for a particular purpose or profession.
The framework or skeleton upon which a new regiment is to be formed; the officers of a regiment forming the staff.
senses.example: The colonel assembled a cadre of officers to form the staff of the new regiment.

core.definition: A small core group of trained, committed people who lead or carry out an important task within an organization.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAH, and say the second as 'dray.' Many Americans also say 'KAD-ree,' especially in military or political talk, so both are accepted.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a trained, committed inner group, and it can sound slightly political or military depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cadre in news, politics, the military, and organizational talk, such as 'a cadre of experienced engineers.' In everyday conversation it sounds formal, so 'core team' or 'group' is more natural. In the US it is also used for a small group of activists or party leaders.

distinctions.note: A team is any working group; a cadre is a small, specially trained core that leads or sets up the larger group.
A faction is a divided subgroup with its own interests; cadre is neutral and suggests a trained, organized core.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is part of the cadre of volunteers who run the community garden every spring.
examples.professional: We need a cadre of two or three senior data engineers who can train the rest of the team on the new pipeline.
examples.analytical: Lenin's theory of the vanguard party relied on a disciplined cadre to convert mass discontent into organized action.

nuance.analogy: Like the stage crew at a theater, a small, skilled group that makes the whole production work.
nuance.etymology: From French cadre 'frame,' from Italian quadro, from Latin quadrum 'square.'
common_mistakes: Using cadre to mean any group of people; it implies a small, trained core.
Pronouncing it like 'cadger' or stressing the second syllable.

cadre.etymology: Borrowed from French *cadre*, from Italian *quadro* (“framed painting, square”), from Latin *quadrum*, from *quattuor* (“four”).

senses.definition: To determine the value of something or the solution to something by a mathematical process.
senses.example: Calculate the square root of 3 to 10 decimal places.

senses.definition: To determine values or solutions by a mathematical process; reckon.
senses.example: She calculated the monthly payment using the loan's interest rate and term.

senses.definition: To ascertain or predict by mathematical or astrological computations the time, circumstances, or other conditions of; to forecast or compute the character or consequences of.
senses.example: to calculate or cast one’s nativity

senses.definition: To adjust for purpose; to adapt by forethought or calculation; to fit or prepare by the adaptation of means to an end.
senses.example: to calculate a system of laws for the government and protection of a free people

senses.definition: To imagine sequences of potential moves and responses without actually moving the pieces.
senses.example: Before moving his knight, the grandmaster calculated several lines three moves deep.

core.definition: To find a number or result by using mathematics, or to estimate something by careful reasoning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a reduced "kyuh" rather than a full "kyoo." Americans do not pronounce the middle as "kyoo-late" with a long vowel. The final syllable rhymes with "late."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes careful mathematical or logical work and can sound precise or cold depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calculate in math class, business, science, and everyday planning, such as calculating a tip or a trip time. In casual speech people often say figure out or work out. Calculate can also mean planning on purpose, as in "she calculated her words," which sounds deliberate.

distinctions.note: Compute often means using a machine or formal procedure to get a result; calculate can be done by hand or in the head.
Estimate means to judge roughly without exact computation, while calculate implies a more exact process.
Figure out is informal and everyday; calculate is more precise and often used in technical or formal work.

examples.everyday: Can you calculate the tip for this bill? I always mess up the math.
examples.professional: Can you calculate the expected cost of the cloud migration before Thursday's meeting?
examples.analytical: The theologian argued that one cannot simply calculate moral worth from outward results, because motives also matter.

nuance.analogy: To calculate is like following a recipe with exact measurements: each step leads to a definite result.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin calculare, to count with pebbles, from calculus, a small stone used for counting.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as "kyoo" with a long vowel; use a reduced "kyuh."
Using calculate for a simple guess; in American English, guess or estimate is more natural unless you are doing a real computation.

calculate.etymology: Latin *calculātus*, perfect passive participle of *calculō* (“to reckon, compute, calculate”) (see *-ate*), from *calculus* (“a pebble”), further from *calx* + *-ulus*.

senses.definition: A word used to represent a cardinal number.

core.definition: A word that names a cardinal number, such as one, two, three or twelve.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have a strong first syllable, KAHR and NOO, and the endings -al and -al are reduced to 'ul'. Americans say the u in numeral as 'oo', not 'you'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a grammar term.
nuance.usage_note: This is mainly a grammar and linguistics term used in school, language courses and translation. Americans in ordinary conversation would just say number word or the number itself. Use cardinal numeral when you need the grammatical category.

distinctions.note: A cardinal number is the abstract quantity, such as five, while a cardinal numeral is the word or symbol used to write it.
An ordinal numeral shows order, like fifth, while a cardinal numeral shows quantity, like five.

examples.everyday: My daughter's worksheet asked her to spell out the cardinal numeral twelve in letters.
examples.professional: For the translation tool, we need to map each cardinal numeral in the source text to the correct number format.
examples.analytical: A cardinal numeral like three is often classified as a determiner, which is why it can come directly before a noun in English.

nuance.analogy: Like a price tag that states an amount, not the item's place in line.
nuance.etymology: Cardinal from Latin cardinalis, meaning principal; numeral from Latin numeralis, relating to number.
common_mistakes: Confusing cardinal numeral with cardinal number; the numeral is the word or symbol, while the number is the quantity itself.
Pronouncing the u in numeral as 'you'; American speech usually says NOO-muh-rul.

senses.definition: Money in the form of notes or bills and coins, as opposed to checks, credit or electronic transactions.
senses.example: How are you off for cash? After you bounced those checks last time, they want to be paid in cash.

senses.definition: Liquid assets, money that can be traded quickly, as distinct from assets that are invested and cannot be easily exchanged.
senses.example: Keep some cash on hand in case the card readers at the market go down.

senses.definition: Money.
Cash register, or the counter in a business where the cash register is located.
senses.example: Let me just bring these to the cash for you.

senses.definition: An instance of winning a cash prize.
senses.example: Her first cash from the poetry contest paid for a long-overdue road trip.

senses.definition: (historical) The low-denomination coin of southern India until 1818.
senses.example: Colonial records list the small cash coin as the standard unit for village wages.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) Any of several similar coins in Southeast and East Asia, particularly the imperial Chinese copper coin.
senses.example: The traveler kept a string of copper cash, threaded with a square hole, in his sleeve.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To exchange (a check/check) for money in the form of notes/bills.
senses.example: I cashed the paycheck at the bank before lunch so I could pay rent.

senses.definition: To obtain a payout from a tournament.
senses.example: Only the top three players cashed in the tournament, which drew a huge crowd.

senses.definition: To disband. To do away with, to kill.
senses.example: The gang boss decided to cash the crew after the failed heist.

senses.definition: Great; excellent; cool.
senses.example: Dude, that new bike you built is totally cash, you should sell it.

core.definition: Money in the form of bills and coins, as opposed to checks, credit cards, or electronic payments.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a of 'cat' and end with the sh sound. Avoid lengthening the vowel into 'kahsh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for money, though it can suggest a quick or unrecorded transaction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say cash for bills and coins in everyday life, as in 'Do you take cash?' or 'I don't have any cash on me'. In a shop, the question 'Cash or card?' is very common. Cash can also mean money in general in informal speech.

distinctions.note: Money is the general term and includes bank deposits and digital payments, while cash refers to physical bills and coins.
Change is the coins or bills returned to you after paying more than the price, while cash is the money you hand over.
Currency is the official system of money, such as dollars, while cash is the physical form of it.

examples.everyday: Do you take cash, or should I pay by card?
examples.professional: Can you pay the venue deposit by check, or do we need to use the company card instead of cash?
examples.analytical: A cash economy leaves a thinner record of transactions than one built on electronic payments.

nuance.analogy: Cash is like a paper map: you can hold it in your hand and see exactly how much you have.
nuance.etymology: From Old French casse, meaning money box, from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa, meaning box.
common_mistakes: Using cash to mean only paper bills, when coins are also cash.
Confusing cash with change, which is the money returned to you after a payment.

cash.etymology: From late Middle French *caisse* (“money-box”), itself borrowed from Occitan *caissa*, from Latin *capsa* (“box”), ultimately from *capiō* (“take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European **kap-* (“grasp”).

senses.definition: Initialism of carbon copy.
senses.example: I had meant to cc you on this earlier. Please reply by next Thursday. Thanks.

senses.definition: Initialism of courtesy copy.
Initialism of closed caption or closed captioning.
senses.example: Please turn on CC so I can follow the dialogue while the volume is muted.

senses.definition: Initialism of cubic centimeter.
senses.example: This plastic syringe delivers one cc of medicine to the mouth of the animal. The medicine is peanut-flavored.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of chapters.
Initialism of carbon copy (“to add an additional recipient to the CC line of an e-mail message”).
senses.example: Please CC your manager on the email so she sees the revised budget too.

senses.definition: Initialism of crowd control.
senses.example: Just cc him, bro.

core.definition: The email field listing people who receive a copy for information, or the abbreviation for carbon copy or courtesy copy.

pronunciation.tip: Say the two letters, 'see' and 'see', with the stress on the second letter. Do not say 'kay-kay' as the letter C is pronounced 'see' in English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Being copied can signal that someone is being kept informed, or that a complaint is being escalated, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cc' almost daily in workplace email. 'Cc' is also used as a verb, as in 'I cc'd my manager'. Recipients on the cc line are usually expected to read but not reply, and hidden recipients go in the bcc field.

distinctions.note: Recipients on bcc, or blind carbon copy, are hidden from the others, while cc recipients are visible to everyone on the email.
People in the 'to' field are expected to act or respond, while people in the cc field are usually just kept informed.

examples.everyday: Can you cc me on the sign-up sheet so I get the updates?
examples.professional: I will cc Priya since she owns the budget decision.
examples.analytical: Copying a supervisor with cc changes the email's social meaning, signaling escalation rather than simple information-sharing.

nuance.analogy: A cc line is like a list of people copied on a memo so they know what happened, even though they are not responsible for acting on it.
nuance.etymology: From carbon copy, a duplicate made with carbon paper, where 'carbon' comes from Latin carbo, 'charcoal'.
common_mistakes: Using 'cc' as a verb without the past form 'cc'd' or a clear phrase like 'copy in'.
Pronouncing the letters as 'kay-kay' instead of 'see-see'.

senses.definition: To perfume with incense.

core.definition: To burn incense before or around a person, object, or altar as an act of worship or honor.

pronunciation.tip: It sounds exactly like 'sense' and 'cents,' one syllable. Do not add a vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and reverent; it belongs to liturgical description.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly in liturgical contexts in Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican churches. In ordinary American English, people say 'burn incense' or 'swing the censer.' Because it sounds like 'sense,' it is rarely heard in conversation.

distinctions.note: As a verb, 'incense' is in this sense usually the substance or the act of burning it, and also, with stress on the second syllable, means to anger someone.
Perfume refers to a general fragrance, while cense is specifically ritual burning of incense.
Fumigate means to disinfect with smoke or gas, not to honor.

examples.everyday: At the Easter service, the priest walked around and censed the whole church.
examples.professional: The rubrics direct the deacon to cense the Gospel book before the reading.
examples.analytical: To cense the icons is to honor the person depicted, and the smoke signifies prayers rising to God.

nuance.analogy: Censing is like letting prayer become visible, as smoke rising upward.
nuance.etymology: Shortened from Middle English incensen, from Old French encenser, from Late Latin incensum, 'something burned.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'sense,' 'cents,' or 'censor.'
Mistaking it for the verb 'incense,' meaning to anger.
Adding an extra vowel, saying 'sen-suh.'
nuance.biblical_note: Burning incense is part of worship in Exodus 30:7-8, where Aaron burns fragrant incense on the altar each morning and evening. Luke 1:9-10 describes Zechariah entering the temple to burn incense while the people prayed outside. Revelation 8:3-4 shows incense mingled with the prayers of the saints.

senses.definition: The process in which mixtures are separated using the centripetal force generated by spinning in a centrifuge.

core.definition: The process of separating the parts of a mixture by spinning it very fast in a centrifuge, so denser parts settle outward.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on GAY, not on the first syllable. The u in fu is pronounced fyoo, not foo, and the final -tion is a soft shuhn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used as a neutral description of a laboratory step.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use centrifugation mainly in labs, medicine, biology, and chemistry, often in written protocols. In everyday speech, people say they spun the sample in a centrifuge or the sample was spun down. The word names the process, not the machine.

distinctions.note: Centrifugation is the process, while a centrifuge is the machine that performs it.
Sedimentation is settling under gravity over time, while centrifugation uses spinning force to speed up that separation.
Filtration separates particles by passing a mixture through a barrier, while centrifugation separates them by density.

examples.everyday: The nurse said your blood sample goes through centrifugation first, so the results should be ready by Friday.
examples.professional: Please add a centrifugation step before the plasma assay to remove the cell debris from the samples.
examples.analytical: Density gradient centrifugation separates organelles by their equilibrium density, so the resolution of the method depends on the gradient's shape.

nuance.analogy: Like a salad spinner that works so hard it sorts sand from water in seconds.
nuance.etymology: From centrifuge plus -ation, from Latin centrum 'center' and fugere 'to flee'.
common_mistakes: Using centrifugation to mean the machine instead of the process; say a centrifuge for the device.
Shifting the stress to the first syllable, as in SEN-trih-FYOO-gay-shun, which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: The advocacy of a centripetal state.
senses.example: Her dissertation defended centripetalism, arguing that ethnic parties should be rewarded for cooperating across lines.

core.definition: The political view that a divided state should be built by rewarding cooperation across groups, to pull the political center together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRIP, the third syllable of the word. Pronounce the -al ending as a reduced uhl, and the last -ism as iz-uhm.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and academic. It names a policy position in political science and is used in debates over constitutional design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use centripetalism mainly in political science, constitutional scholarship, and policy discussions about divided societies. It is rare in everyday conversation. Scholars often contrast it with consociationalism, which emphasizes power-sharing among group leaders.

distinctions.note: Centrism is a moderate political position between left and right, while centripetalism is a specific approach to designing institutions in divided states.
Consociationalism distributes power among group leaders, while centripetalism tries to encourage moderate, cross-group politics.

examples.professional: Our policy memo recommends centripetalism for the electoral reform, since the ballot rules would reward candidates who win votes across groups.
examples.analytical: Centripetalism claims that institutional design can pull parties toward the center, though critics doubt that it reduces ethnic conflict over time.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge built to pull two riverbanks together rather than keep them apart.
nuance.etymology: From centripetal plus -ism, from Latin centrum 'center' and petere 'to seek'.
common_mistakes: Confusing centripetalism with centrism, which is a moderate political position rather than an institutional design theory.
Placing the stress on the first syllable instead of TRIP.

senses.definition: A distress of mind caused by a failure of aims or plans, a want of appreciation, mistakes, etc. vexation or mortification.
senses.example: much to the chagrin (of)

senses.definition: A type of leather or skin with a rough surface.
senses.example: The antique jewelry box was covered in green chagrin, its rough surface cool to the touch.

senses.definition: To bother or vex; to mortify.
senses.example: Her dismissive comment about the poem chagrined the young poet, who had hoped for praise.

core.definition: A feeling of embarrassment, annoyance, or disappointment, especially after a failure or mistake.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, not the first as in the dictionary form. The ch is pronounced sh, and the g is hard before the r, so say shuh-GRIN, not CHAG-rin.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Chagrin implies you are disappointed or embarrassed, often in yourself, so it describes an unpleasant reaction to a failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chagrin mostly in writing, speeches, or polished storytelling, not in casual talk. The common pattern is 'to my chagrin' or 'much to his chagrin,' followed by the event that caused the feeling. Casual speakers would more often say embarrassed or annoyed.

distinctions.note: Embarrassment is the feeling of being seen as foolish; chagrin is more about disappointment at a failed plan, often mixed with irritation at yourself.
Disappointment is general and can come from outside events; chagrin adds a sense of having been outdone or humiliated, usually by your own mistake.

examples.everyday: To my chagrin, I left my phone at the restaurant and had to drive back to get it.
examples.professional: To our chagrin, the launch slipped two weeks because we missed a dependency in the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: The author's chagrin at his own flawed argument reveals how closely his self-image depended on being right.

nuance.analogy: Like walking into a meeting with your shirt on inside out: the irritation is mixed with self-blame.
nuance.etymology: From French chagrin, meaning sorrow or vexation; the exact origin of the French word is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (CHAG-rin), which makes it hard to understand
Using chagrin for a mild annoyance; it implies some embarrassment or disappointment with yourself
Using chagrin as a casual verb; Americans more often say I was chagrined or to my chagrin

chagrin.etymology: From French *chagrin* (“sorrow”), from Middle French *chagrin* (“pain, affliction”) (compare, *chagrigner* (“to experience sorrow”), ), probably derived from *chagreiner*, *chagraigner* (“to sadden”), of origin.

senses.definition: Having the characteristics of a chameleon.
senses.example: The politician's chameleon-like views shifted with every audience, so nobody knew what he believed.

core.definition: Able to change your appearance, behavior or opinions to suit the situation, often in a way that seems insincere.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the mee syllable of chameleon, and like keeps a secondary stress, so do not reduce it to lick. Also, the ch is a k sound, not ch as in church.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it can praise adaptability, but often suggests a lack of firm principles.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chameleon-like to describe people who fit into any group or change opinions to suit the room. It is more often a mild criticism than a compliment, especially in politics or business. Americans more often say He's a real chameleon, and the adjective works well in writing or formal analysis.

distinctions.note: Versatile is positive and emphasizes range of skills, while chameleon-like suggests changing to match surroundings, which can seem insincere.
Adaptable is neutral to positive and describes flexibility, while chameleon-like often implies a lack of firm principles.
Two-faced is strongly negative and means deceitful, while chameleon-like is milder and describes adjusting to others.

examples.everyday: My roommate is so chameleon-like that she fits in with any group of friends.
examples.professional: The product manager's chameleon-like style let her adapt to every client, though the team wanted clearer principles.
examples.analytical: Some readers find the narrator's chameleon-like voice compelling, but it also makes his moral position hard to pin down.

nuance.analogy: Like a chameleon on a branch, taking on the colors of whatever it sits near.
nuance.etymology: From chameleon, from Greek khamaileōn meaning ground lion, plus -like.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch as the ch in church instead of a k sound.
Stressing like too heavily or reducing it to a short lick sound.

senses.definition: A two-wheeled horse-drawn cart, used in Bronze Age and Early Iron Age warfare.
senses.example: The warriors rode into battle on a horse-drawn chariot.

senses.definition: A light (four-wheeled) carriage used for ceremonial or pleasure purposes.
The rook piece.
senses.example: In the Xiangqi game, my opponent's chariot trapped my general along the open file.

senses.definition: To ride in a chariot.
senses.example: Every summer the pageant organizers chariot the queen through the crowded streets of the old town.

senses.definition: (rare, poetic) To convey by, or as if by, chariot.
senses.example: Faith chariots the weary soul home across the stormy sea of grief.
senses.label: rare, poetic

core.definition: A two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in ancient warfare, or a light carriage used for ceremonies and rides.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending is a weak 'ee-uht' rather than 'ee-ot'. Many learners say 'CHAT-ee-ot' or add an extra syllable. The 'ch' is one sound, and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest grandeur, speed, or ancient warfare, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use chariot in historical, biblical, or literary contexts, such as Roman chariot races or a royal procession. In everyday speech you would more likely say car, carriage, or cart. The phrase 'Chariots of Fire' is a well-known film title, and the word also appears in sports and advertising for dramatic effect.

distinctions.note: A carriage is a horse-drawn passenger vehicle for ordinary travel, while a chariot is a light, fast vehicle used in war, racing, or ceremony.
A cart is a plain vehicle for carrying goods, often pulled by a horse or ox, and it has no ceremonial or military associations.

examples.everyday: My kids loved the movie about the chariot race in ancient Rome.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit includes a restored bronze chariot from the Iron Age, and the curators are writing the placard text now.
examples.analytical: The chariot in Egyptian military texts functioned as a symbol of royal power as well as a tactical weapon.

nuance.analogy: A chariot is like a sports car of the ancient world: fast, light, and built for a driver and a purpose rather than comfort.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'char', from Latin 'carrus', a wheeled vehicle, of Celtic origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'CHAT-ee-ot' with the first syllable like 'chat' instead of 'chair'.
Using chariot for an ordinary car in casual speech, which sounds odd or humorous.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is merkāḇâ, meaning chariot, and the Egyptian and Canaanite war chariot is central to the Exodus story. In Genesis 41:43 Pharaoh has Joseph ride in his second chariot as a sign of honor. In Exodus 14:25 the wheels of the Egyptian chariots come off as the army pursues Israel into the sea. In 2 Kings 2:11 Elijah is taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire, a striking image of divine transport.

chariot.etymology: From Middle English *chariot*, from Old French *chariot*, from *char* (“cart”), from Latin *carrus* (“wagon”), itself borrowed from **karros*, from **karros* (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European **ḱr̥sós*.

senses.definition: The noisy banging of pots and pans as a mock serenade to a newly married couple, or similar occasion.
Any loud, cacophonous noise or hubbub.
senses.example: The wedding guests set off a charivari of pots, pans, and car horns outside the newlyweds' house.

core.definition: A noisy, mock celebration, traditionally banging pots and pans, held to tease a newly married couple; any loud, chaotic din.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VAHR, and the initial ch is an sh sound inherited from French. The final syllable is a light ee, not a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It describes a rowdy, teasing celebration, often humorous or mildly mocking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use charivari in everyday speech; it is a rare, literary word found in older writing or descriptions of folk custom. For a noisy party or commotion, people say racket, din, or commotion. If you do use it, a humorous tone fits best.

distinctions.note: A racket is a common word for loud noise; charivari is rarer and specifically suggests a noisy, mock celebration.
Cacophony is a formal word for harsh, discordant sound; charivari suggests a festive, rowdy occasion.

examples.everyday: The neighbors made a charivari outside the newlyweds' house, banging pots until the couple came out laughing.
examples.professional: Launch night turned into a charivari of cheering and noisemakers, so the manager had to call a short break.
examples.analytical: Historians of folk custom describe the charivari as a community's public way of policing unusual or disapproved marriages.

nuance.analogy: Like a parade of clanging pans that turns a wedding into a street band.
nuance.etymology: From French, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial ch as a hard ch, as in cheese; it is an sh sound.
Using charivari for any noise; it refers to a rowdy, mock celebration rather than noise alone.

senses.definition: Talk, especially meaningless or unimportant talk.
senses.example: Her speech was full of idle chatter about celebrity gossip and the weather.

senses.definition: The sound of talking.
senses.example: From the kitchen came the chatter of the kids and the clatter of dishes.

senses.definition: The vocalisations of a Eurasian magpie, Pica pica.
senses.example: Early each morning, a magpie's sharp chatter echoed across the orchard fence.

senses.definition: The vocalisations of various birds or other animals.
senses.example: Under the eaves, the squirrels set up a noisy chatter whenever the cat appeared.

senses.definition: An intermittent noise, as from vibration.
senses.example: Proper brake adjustment will help to reduce the chatter.

senses.definition: In national security, the degree of communication between suspect groups and individuals, used to gauge the degree of expected terrorist activity.
senses.example: The NSA is concerned about increased chatter between known terror groups.

senses.definition: The situation where a drill or similar tool vibrates and tears the material rather than cutting it cleanly.
senses.example: The drill bit started to chatter, so I slowed the feed rate and eased off the pressure.

senses.definition: A group of songbirds.
senses.example: We watched a chatter of waxwings settle into the crabapple tree at dusk.

senses.definition: One who chats.
senses.example: Dad was the chatter of the family, always the first to start a conversation.

senses.definition: A user of livestream chat.
senses.example: The streamer thanked every chatter who donated during tonight's charity broadcast.

senses.definition: A user of chat rooms.
senses.example: Old chatters in that forum still remember the server outage from 2003.

senses.definition: To talk idly.
senses.example: They knitted and chattered the whole time.

senses.definition: To make a noise by rapid collisions.
senses.example: He was so cold that his teeth were chattering.

senses.definition: To utter sounds which somewhat resemble language, but are inarticulate and indistinct.
senses.example: The toddler would chatter happily to her stuffed rabbit during bath time.

core.definition: To talk quickly and casually about small, unimportant things, often in a lively way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. In American speech the middle t is a flap, so it sounds close to 'CHAD-er', and the final syllable is a reduced 'er'. Do not pronounce a hard, full t sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it suggests talk that is light, lively, or unimportant, and can sound annoying if constant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chatter for light conversation, especially among friends, children, or in a crowded room. 'Chatter' can be a complaint, as in 'stop the chatter.' For a neutral description of talk, people often say chat. Used as a noun, chatter often means a noisy buzz of voices.

distinctions.note: Chat is the friendlier, more neutral word for casual conversation, while chatter often suggests noisy or pointless talk.
Gossip is talk about other people's private lives, while chatter can be about anything trivial.

examples.everyday: The kids were chattering about the game the whole car ride home.
examples.professional: Please keep the chatter down during the call, because the client is trying to listen.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that much public debate is mere chatter, rather than reasoned exchange.

nuance.analogy: Chatter is like background static on a radio: a constant noise that is often pleasant but carries little meaning.
nuance.etymology: Imitative in origin, from Middle English 'chateren', imitating rapid, repeated sounds.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle t as a hard, clear t instead of the flap, which sounds more natural in American speech.
Using chatter as a countable noun in a way that sounds strange, such as 'a chatter' for a single conversation.

chatter.etymology: From Middle English *chateren*, from earlier *cheteren*, *chiteren* (“to twitter, chatter, jabber”), of origin.

senses.definition: In a cheeky or impudent manner.

core.definition: In a playful, slightly bold or disrespectful way that is more amusing than offensive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, CHEE-kih-lee. The second syllable is a short, weak vowel, not a long ee, so the ending sounds like 'lee' only at the very end.

nuance.connotation: Mildly positive or playful. It can suggest affection, but it can also sound slightly rude depending on the situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans understand cheekily, but it is more common in British English, and Americans often say sassily, saucily, or fresh instead. It is used in casual conversation and to describe a child, pet, or friend who is teasing in a bold way. In formal settings, avoid it because it suggests disrespect.

distinctions.note: Sassily is a more common American word and can sound more directly disrespectful than cheekily.
Impudently is formal and stronger, and it suggests real rudeness rather than playful boldness.

examples.everyday: The little boy looked at his grandma and cheekily asked for dessert before dinner.
examples.professional: Ray cheekily suggested we move the deadline to Friday, and the room laughed.
examples.analytical: Socrates often questioned his interlocutors cheekily, but his aim was always to expose inconsistency.

nuance.analogy: Like a friend who makes a joke at your expense with a grin, so you laugh rather than get angry.
nuance.etymology: From cheeky, from cheek in the sense of impudence, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using cheekily in formal writing, where it sounds too casual.
Confusing cheekily with cheerily, which means happily.

senses.definition: In a chivalrous manner.

core.definition: In a courteous, gallant way, showing respect and protection, especially toward women and those in need.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable. The -al and -ous endings are weak, reduced vowels, so the word has about four light syllables after the stress. The final -ly is 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises courtesy and protectiveness, although some people see the gender assumptions behind chivalrous behavior as outdated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chivalrously in writing and formal description, such as a news report or a novel. In everyday speech they more often say politely, courteously, or just 'He held the door for me.' It can sound a bit old-fashioned or ironic when used about modern manners.

distinctions.note: Politely is the everyday word for good manners, while chivalrously adds the sense of gallant, protective respect.
Courteously is more formal and general, while chivalrously suggests a gentlemanly or protective attitude.
Gallantly suggests brave or stylish courtesy, often with a literary or romantic tone.

examples.everyday: He chivalrously carried the groceries to my car, even though I told him I could manage.
examples.professional: She chivalrously took the blame in the meeting so the junior engineer would not be criticized.
examples.analytical: The poem's hero behaves chivalrously toward his defeated rival, sparing his life and returning his horse.

nuance.analogy: Acting chivalrously is like holding an umbrella over someone else before you think about your own dry shoes.
nuance.etymology: From chivalrous, from chivalry, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'chive' instead of 'chiv', as in 'chivalry'.
Using chivalrously in casual speech where politely is more natural.

senses.definition: A two-dimensional geometric figure, a line, consisting of the set of all those points in a plane that are equally distant from a given point (center).
senses.example: The set of all points (x, y) such that (x − 1) + y = r is a circle of radius r around the point (1, 0).
