Stressing the second syllable (sor-TER) instead of the first.

senses.definition: The direction or area lying to the south of a place.
Situated or directed towards the south; moving or facing towards the south.
Towards the south; in a southerly direction.

core.definition: Toward the south; in the direction of the south.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending -ward is unstressed and reduced to a short r-colored vowel. Do not add an extra syllable after the th.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use southward mainly in descriptions of movement, such as weather systems, migrating birds or routes on a map. In casual speech, people more often say 'south' alone, as in 'We drove south.' Southward is slightly more formal and descriptive.

distinctions.note: South is the everyday adverb for direction; southward is more descriptive and often appears in written or formal style.
Southerly describes wind or direction coming from or toward the south; southward describes movement toward it.

examples.everyday: The storm is slowly moving southward, so we might lose power tonight.
examples.professional: Our logistics team is shifting the warehouse inventory southward to the Atlanta distribution center.
examples.analytical: The author traces the migration of the tribe southward across the plains over several generations.

nuance.analogy: Like an arrow on a compass pointing down toward the bottom of the map.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sūth (south) and -weard (toward).
common_mistakes: Using 'southward' as a noun for the south; the noun is 'the south'.
Adding a syllable, saying 'SOWTH-ward-ayz' instead of ending with a reduced vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind 'southward' is negeb (Hebrew נֶגֶב), meaning dry land or the south, the arid region south of Judah. Genesis 12:9 describes Abram journeying on by stages toward the Negeb. Genesis 13:1 says Abram went up from Egypt into the Negeb. These passages show the Negeb as a region of direction and movement in the patriarchal narratives.

senses.definition: Having widely spaced intervals.
senses.example: a sparse array, index, or matrix

senses.definition: Not dense; meager; scanty.
senses.example: The sparse crowd at the early game left plenty of empty seats.

senses.definition: Having few nonzero elements.

core.definition: Having few nonzero entries, so most values in a dataset or matrix are zero.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a rhotic r, so pronounce the r clearly before the s. Do not add a vowel between the r and the s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In general speech it can suggest a shortage or thinness, while in technical writing it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sparse both in everyday speech for thinly spread things, such as sparse crowds or sparse furniture, and in data science and mathematics for data with mostly zero values. In technical talk, saying the data is sparse is a normal, precise description. For a general shortage, scarce is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Scarce means hard to find or in short supply, while sparse means thinly spread or not dense across a space or set.
Dense is the opposite: many items or nonzero values are packed close together.

examples.everyday: The town is sparse in the winter, so the diner is pretty quiet most days.
examples.professional: Our user-item matrix is very sparse, so we should use a sparse data format to save memory.
examples.analytical: A sparse signal is one in which most components vanish, and this assumption makes high-dimensional recovery possible.

nuance.analogy: A sparse matrix is like a parking lot where only a few spaces have cars and the rest are empty.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sparsus, past participle of spargere, meaning to scatter.
common_mistakes: Confusing sparse with scarce when talking about a general shortage.
Saying sparsy or sparsed instead of sparse.

senses.definition: A person who spells.
senses.example: I'm a slow reader but a good speller.

senses.definition: A participant in a spelling bee.
A book used to learn how to spell properly.
senses.example: My grandmother kept an old speller on the shelf, and we practiced words from it every evening.

senses.definition: A spell checker.

core.definition: A person who spells words, especially a contestant in a spelling bee.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on SPEL. The double l is one consonant sound, and the last syllable is a reduced American r-colored schwa, so say SPEL-ur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it becomes a compliment when describing someone's skill, such as 'a good speller'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use speller for someone who spells well or poorly, and especially for children in school spelling bees. It can also name a textbook, but in everyday talk it almost always means a person. A natural compliment is 'You're a great speller, you should enter the bee.'

distinctions.note: A speller is a person, while a spell checker is software that flags spelling errors.
An orthographer is a specialist in writing systems, while speller is an everyday word for someone who spells.

examples.everyday: My daughter is a strong speller, so she's already practicing for the school bee.
examples.professional: I'm a fairly careful speller, but I still run every proposal through the editor before it goes out.
examples.analytical: A good speller often recognizes a word's Latin or Greek root before consulting any dictionary.

nuance.analogy: Like a pianist who plays by ear, a skilled speller just knows how words sound and look together.
nuance.etymology: From spell plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who spells.
common_mistakes: Confusing speller, the person, with spelling, the act or the correct written form.
Pronouncing the last syllable as a full vowel, saying SPEL-ler, instead of a reduced American r-sound.

senses.definition: In the manner of a sphere or globe.

core.definition: In the shape of a sphere, or in a way that is equal in all directions like a sphere or globe.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The word is three syllables, not four, because the middle syllable -ic- is quick and the final -ly is 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is used in descriptive and technical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use spherically in conversation. You will see it in scientific or technical writing, such as spherically symmetric. In everyday speech, people say round or perfectly round.

distinctions.note: Circularly describes motion or arrangement in a circle on a flat plane. Spherically describes three-dimensional shape or distribution.
Evenly means equally spread out. Spherically means equally distributed in all three dimensions around a center.

examples.everyday: Those cotton balls are shaped almost spherically, so they roll when you drop them.
examples.professional: The sensor array is spherically distributed, so the coverage should be even in every direction.
examples.analytical: A spherically symmetric potential depends only on the distance from the center, not on the direction of approach.

nuance.analogy: Like a drop of water floating in zero gravity, which takes a spherical shape evenly in every direction.
nuance.etymology: Formed from spherical with the adverb suffix -ly; spherical comes from Greek sphaira, meaning 'ball'.
common_mistakes: Using spherically for everyday roundness, where Americans say round.
Adding an extra syllable and saying 'sfair-ih-kuh-lee' instead of the three-syllable 'SFAIR-ik-lee'.

senses.definition: To disclose information, especially of a sensitive nature.
senses.example: My coworker finally decided to spill the tea about the office budget cuts.

core.definition: To share gossip or private information about other people, usually in a lively, interested way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'tea', and 'spill' gets lighter secondary stress. The word 'the' reduces to 'thuh' before the consonant, so the phrase sounds like 'spil-thuh-TEE'.

nuance.connotation: Playful and informal, usually friendly. It can be negative if the gossip is cruel or private, so use it carefully about people who are not present.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spill the tea in casual conversation with friends, often as a playful request such as 'Okay, spill the tea!' It became popular through social media and Black American and LGBTQ+ communities, so you will hear it often on TV and online. A natural reply is 'Okay, so here's what happened...' Avoid it at work or with people you do not know well.

distinctions.note: Gossip is the general word for talking about others, while spill the tea is a playful, informal request for the juicy details.
Tell me everything is a warm, general request for details, while spill the tea suggests gossip or scandal.

examples.everyday: Okay, you met him last night, so spill the tea!
examples.professional: I shouldn't spill the tea about the reorg, but leadership is changing the team structure next quarter.
examples.analytical: Gossip networks act as informal information systems, and when people spill the tea, they reveal the unwritten norms of an organization.

nuance.analogy: Spilling the tea is like opening a sealed envelope that everyone else is curious about.
common_mistakes: Taking the phrase literally as talk about a drink; in American slang it means sharing gossip.
Using it in formal settings, where it sounds too casual.

synonyms: let the cat out of the bag
spill-the-tea.etymology: Originally from *spill the T*, standing for *truth*, which evolved into *tea*.

inflections: spilled the tea, spilt the tea

senses.definition: Synonym of spittoon.

core.definition: A small container for spitting into, such as a spittoon, often used in baseball dugouts or by people who chew tobacco or sunflower seeds.

pronunciation.tip: The dictionary marks stress on the second word, but Americans stress the first word of this compound noun: SPIT-cup. The vowel in cup is the short uh sound, not the oo of 'cop'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical, though the object itself suggests unsanitary habits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say spit cup mainly in baseball and other sports, where players chew sunflower seeds or tobacco and need somewhere to spit. Outside sports, people often say spittoon, especially for old-fashioned containers. Spitting on the floor is considered rude and unsanitary, so use the cup when one is provided.

distinctions.note: The two words mean the same thing, but spittoon sounds older and more formal, while spit cup is modern and casual.

collocations: a spit cup in the dugout
a spit cup for sunflower seeds

examples.everyday: Please don't spit on the sidewalk; there's a spit cup by the bench.
examples.professional: Facilities asked us to keep spit cups out of the lab because of the sanitation rules.
examples.analytical: The phrase spit cup reflects a shift from the Victorian spittoon to a disposable, sanitary container.

nuance.analogy: Like a small trash can built only for spit.
nuance.etymology: A compound of spit (from Old English spittan) and cup.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second word, saying spit-CUP, which marks the phrase rather than the compound noun.
Using spit cup for a drinking cup or a sink, which is a different object.

senses.definition: (poetic) Bread or some other staple foodstuff.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: Bread, or another basic food that people depend on every day for nourishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAFF and LIFE, and of reduces to a quick uhv or uh in speech. The f in staff is unvoiced, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: it presents bread as a basic, life-sustaining food and sounds elevated in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in writing, speeches, sermons, and historical or literary contexts, not in casual conversation. In everyday talk, people simply say bread or a staple food. The phrase is usually used with the and describes a food that a whole society relies on.

distinctions.note: A staple is any basic, regularly used food or product; staff of life is a poetic phrase reserved for bread or grain as sustenance.
In this phrase staff is an old word for a stick or support, not the everyday meaning of a group of employees.

collocations: bread as the staff of life
rice as the staff of life
the staff of life for millions

examples.everyday: My grandmother always called bread the staff of life, so she baked a loaf every single morning.
examples.professional: In our food security report, we describe maize as the staff of life for much of the region.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly ties bread to survival, which is why the image of bread as the staff of life carried such weight in ancient communities.

nuance.analogy: Like a sturdy walking stick, it is something you lean on every day to stay upright.
nuance.etymology: From staff (a stick used for support), reflecting the Hebrew image of bread as the support of life in Leviticus 26:26.
common_mistakes: Using staff of life for any food; it is a poetic phrase reserved for basic foods like bread.
Adding words or changing the fixed phrase, such as staff of the life.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the phrase is matteh lechem (מַטֵּה לֶחֶם), where matteh means staff or rod and lechem means bread. In the RSV, Leviticus 26:26 speaks of God breaking the people's staff of bread, meaning their food supply, and Psalm 105:16 describes God breaking every staff of bread during a famine. The image presents bread as the support that holds up human life.

senses.definition: One of a number of narrow strips of wood, or narrow iron plates, placed edge to edge to form the sides, covering, or lining of a vessel or structure; especially, one of the strips which form the sides of a cask, barrel, pail, etc.
senses.example: The cooper replaced a cracked stave on the old oak barrel before the harvest.

senses.definition: One of the bars or rounds of a rack, rungs of a ladder, etc; one of the cylindrical bars of a lantern wheel.
senses.example: The firefighter climbed the ladder, testing each stave before putting weight on it.

senses.definition: A metrical portion; a stanza; a staff.
senses.example: The hymn's final stave was sung slowly by the whole congregation together.

senses.definition: A sign, symbol or sigil, including rune or rune-like characters, used in Icelandic magic.
senses.example: The Icelandic sorcerer carved a protective stave into the wooden door frame.

senses.definition: A staff or walking stick.
senses.example: The old farmer leaned on a knotted stave as he walked the fence line.

senses.definition: The set of five horizontal and parallel lines on and between which musical notes are written or pointed; the staff.
senses.example: She wrote the melody on the stave, then added the chords beneath it.

senses.definition: (rare) The initial consonant, consonant cluster, or vowel of a word which rhymes with another word with the same consonant or vowel in stave-rhyme.
senses.example: The poet's alliterative line used a strong stave to bind its first words together.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To fit or furnish with staves or rundles.
senses.example: We staved the barrel with new oak strips before filling it with wine.

senses.definition: To break in the staves of; to break a hole in; to burst.
senses.example: to stave in a cask

senses.definition: To push, or keep off, as with a staff.
senses.example: He staved off the snapping dog with his walking stick until help arrived.

senses.definition: To delay by force or craft; to drive away.
senses.example: We ate grass in an attempt to stave off our hunger.

senses.definition: To suffer, or cause to be lost by breaking the cask.
senses.example: The careless porter staved the keg and spilled most of the beer.

senses.definition: To render impervious or solid by driving with a calking iron.
senses.example: to stave lead, or the joints of pipes into which lead has been run

core.definition: To prevent or delay something unpleasant, such as defeat, hunger, illness, or a crisis, for a period of time.

pronunciation.tip: The word is one syllable with a voiced final v, not an f sound. In the phrasal verb stave off, the words link and the stress usually falls on off, as in STAYV-OFF.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it concerns avoiding something bad; positive when the thing avoided is harmful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stave off mainly in news and business to describe holding back a threat, as in stave off a recession, stave off hunger, or stave off a cold. It is somewhat formal and usually refers to something bad. In casual talk, people more often say hold off or keep at bay; the barrel-strip sense belongs to woodworking and barrel-making.

distinctions.note: Hold off is more casual and can mean wait; stave off means actively prevent or delay something harmful.
Prevent is a general, neutral word; stave off suggests holding back a threat for a while, not necessarily stopping it entirely.
Delay means to postpone; stave off is used when the thing postponed is unwanted, such as defeat or illness.

examples.everyday: I ate a granola bar to stave off hunger until dinner.
examples.professional: The team cut scope on the feature to stave off a delay in the release.
examples.analytical: Central banks often raise interest rates to stave off inflation, though the trade-off is slower economic growth.

nuance.analogy: Staving off a problem is like holding a door shut against a crowd: you can delay the rush, but you may not stop it.
nuance.etymology: From the noun stave, a staff or strip of wood; the keep-off sense comes from pushing something away with a staff.
common_mistakes: Confusing stave with stay: stave means to prevent or delay, while stay means to remain in a place.
Using stave off for something good; it is used for unwanted events, such as a recession or an illness.

senses.definition: To characterize as disgraceful or ignominious; to mark with a stigma or stigmata.
senses.example: Critics stigmatize the online community as a haven for trolls and conspiracy theorists.

core.definition: To describe or treat a person, group, or condition as shameful or disgraceful, often unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the ending sounds like 'tize' with a long i.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies unfair judgment and harm to the person labeled.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stigmatize' in discussions of social justice, health, and mental illness. It is formal and is most natural in writing or serious talk. In casual speech people say 'put someone down' or 'judge', but 'stigmatize' fits when the unfair social label is the point.

distinctions.note: Criticize means to judge something's flaws; stigmatize means to attach lasting shame to someone or a group.
Label is neutral; stigmatize implies a harmful, shaming label.

examples.everyday: I don't want to stigmatize anyone for needing a break from work.
examples.professional: Calling employees lazy for taking leave only stigmatizes people who need support.
examples.analytical: Labeling a whole community as criminal stigmatizes its members regardless of individual conduct.

nuance.analogy: Like a brand burned into skin, stigmatize leaves a mark that others see first.
nuance.etymology: From stigma with the suffix -ize, meaning to mark or treat as.
common_mistakes: Using 'stigmatize' as a synonym for 'criticize' in everyday contexts.
Mispronouncing the ending, saying 'stig-muh-tighz' with a long a sound.

senses.definition: A substance that acts to increase physiological or nervous activity in the body.
Something that promotes activity, interest, or enthusiasm.
senses.example: Her enthusiasm was a stimulant for the whole team during the long debugging session.

senses.definition: Acting as a stimulant.
senses.example: The lower interest rates had a stimulant effect on local hiring.

core.definition: A substance, such as caffeine, that speeds up physical or nervous activity in the body.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'u' is usually a weak schwa, not a full 'oo', so don't say STIM-yoo-lant. The final -ant is unstressed and sounds like 'unt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical or scientific contexts; often negative when describing drugs, and positive when describing motivation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stimulant' for caffeine, nicotine, and prescription medicines such as those for ADHD. In everyday talk you might say 'Coffee is a stimulant' or 'Energy drinks have a lot of stimulants.' For a motivating person or event, Americans more often say 'a boost' or 'a kick' in casual speech.

distinctions.note: A stimulus is anything that triggers a response; a stimulant is a substance that increases activity.
A depressant slows bodily or nervous activity, which is the opposite effect of a stimulant.

examples.everyday: I can't have a second coffee after lunch because that stimulant keeps me up all night.
examples.professional: The study tracked how each stimulant changed attention scores over six weeks.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that market competition works as a stimulant to innovation, but it can also exhaust the workers it energizes.

nuance.analogy: Like a shot of espresso for the nervous system: it wakes things up but does not feed them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stimulans, meaning stimulating, from stimulare, to goad.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as STIM-yoo-lant; the middle syllable is weak.
Using stimulant as a synonym for stimulus; a stimulus is a trigger, while a stimulant is a substance.

senses.definition: Stitches, collectively.
senses.example: The stitching is coming undone on this shirt.

senses.definition: Synonym of z-fighting.
senses.example: The stitching on the floor textures shimmered because two polygons shared nearly the same depth.

core.definition: Rows or patterns of stitches sewn into fabric, leather or other material, collectively.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending is a short 'ing' with a short 'i' and a clear 'ng,' not a long 'eeng.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes the quality or pattern of stitches, which can be praised or criticized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stitching' in shopping, fashion and product talk, such as 'nice stitching' or 'loose stitching on the seam.' It is usually uncountable and refers to the stitches as a group. In computer graphics, 'stitching' has another meaning, but in everyday speech it refers to sewing.

distinctions.note: A seam is the joined edge of fabric, while stitching is the row of thread that makes it.
Quilting is the process of stitching layers together, often in patterns, while stitching is the general result.

examples.everyday: The jacket looks great, but the stitching is coming loose along the collar.
examples.professional: Our quality checks now measure the stitching density on every bag before shipping.
examples.analytical: The stitching in the old quilt reveals both the maker's skill and the family's history.

nuance.analogy: Like the wiring in a house: you do not see it, but it holds the whole structure together.
nuance.etymology: From stitch (verb) plus the suffix -ing, forming a noun for the act or result of stitching.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'ee' vowel.
Using 'stitchings' as a plural; the word is normally uncountable.

senses.definition: A function that maps elements of an index set to elements of a collection of random variables; historically, a collection of random variables indexed by a set of numbers usually regarded as points in time.
senses.example: In our course on finance, we modeled daily stock returns as a stochastic process with random shocks.

core.definition: A collection of random variables indexed by time or another set, used to model a quantity that evolves randomly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable of 'stochastic' (stuh-KAS-tik), not the first, and keep the first syllable a weak schwa. In 'process,' the stress is on the first syllable, PRAH-ses.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in probability and statistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stochastic process' in mathematics, statistics, finance, physics and data science. 'Random process' is a common synonym in applied work, while 'stochastic process' is preferred in formal probability theory. You would rarely use it in casual talk, but it is common in meetings about models or forecasts.

distinctions.note: A random variable is a single quantity with uncertain value, while a stochastic process is a family of such variables indexed by time or another set.
Random process is a common, less formal synonym, while stochastic process is the standard term in formal probability theory.
Deterministic describes a system whose future is fixed by its current state, with no randomness, which is the contrast to stochastic.

examples.everyday: My commute time feels like a stochastic process, because it changes a little bit every day.
examples.professional: We modeled customer churn as a stochastic process with daily transition probabilities.
examples.analytical: A stochastic process assigns a random variable to each index value, so each realization is a whole function of time rather than a single outcome.

nuance.analogy: Like a random walk on a map: each step is uncertain, but the path follows clear statistical rules.
nuance.etymology: 'Stochastic' from Greek stokhastikos, 'skillful in aiming or guessing'; 'process' from Latin processus, 'a going forward.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'STOH-kas-tik,' instead of 'stuh-KAS-tik.'
Confusing 'stochastic' with 'stoic,' which means calm endurance and has no connection to randomness.

senses.definition: Sickening or disgusting.

core.definition: Extremely unpleasant or disgusting, causing a strong feeling of nausea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, turning, with a strong rhotic r in the first syllable. Keep stomach short and reduced, and do not pronounce the ch.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes things that are very gross, cruel or repulsive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stomach-turning for gross food, bad smells, violent scenes, or someone's cruel behavior. It is vivid and casual, so it fits conversation and reviews. In formal writing, people might use nauseating or revolting instead.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly interchangeable, but stomach-churning is slightly more common and suggests a stronger, more physical churning feeling.
Nauseating is more formal or clinical and describes causing nausea directly, while stomach-turning is more casual and vivid.

examples.everyday: The smell from the dumpster behind the restaurant was absolutely stomach-turning.
examples.professional: The vendor's security report had some stomach-turning details about the old database passwords.
examples.analytical: The novel's most stomach-turning passages are not gratuitous; they reveal how ordinary people normalize cruelty.

nuance.analogy: A stomach-turning sight is like a sudden drop on a roller coaster that makes your stomach lurch.
nuance.etymology: From stomach and turn, the verb, with the participle used as an adjective.
common_mistakes: Omitting the hyphen before a noun, as in 'stomach turning smell'.
Using it as a noun instead of an adjective.
Using it for mild dislike; it implies something quite gross or repulsive.

senses.definition: The crime of killing by strangling.

core.definition: The crime of killing someone by squeezing their throat, or the act of doing so.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a very light, reduced 'guh', so 'gl' sounds almost like one sound, and the final '-ing' is a clear 'ing'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It refers to violent crime.
nuance.usage_note: 'Strangling' as a noun appears mostly in legal reports, medical reports and crime news. In everyday speech, Americans usually say 'strangulation' or use the verb 'strangle'. In a legal context, the charge might be 'assault by strangulation', and the word is widely used in domestic violence training.

distinctions.note: Choking usually means blocking the airway, often by food or an object, while strangling involves squeezing the neck from outside.
'Strangulation' is the more common and formal noun in legal and medical writing, while 'strangling' is more of an action word.

examples.everyday: I can't watch those crime dramas anymore, because the strangling scenes make me too uncomfortable.
examples.professional: Our safety training covers strangling as a warning sign of domestic violence, so staff know when to escalate.
examples.analytical: Strangling is distinctive as a crime because it often leaves little external evidence, yet it requires sustained force.

nuance.analogy: Strangling is like a slow knot pulled tighter: the pressure builds gradually, and the damage is hidden until it is too late.
nuance.etymology: From 'strangle', from Latin 'strangulare' and Greek 'strangalan', meaning to choke.
common_mistakes: Using 'strangling' as an everyday word for something annoying; it refers only to violent crime.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'stran-GLING' instead of 'STRANG-gul-ing'.

senses.definition: Synonym of walk in the park.
senses.example: Finishing the marathon was a stroll in the park for the veteran runner.

core.definition: Something that is very easy to do and needs little effort or skill. It is usually used in the negative.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'park', while 'stroll' has weaker secondary stress. 'In the' is reduced to 'in thuh', and the 'r' in 'park' is strongly rhotic in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means easy, but often negative in usage because people use it to say something was hard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'It was no stroll in the park' to mean a task was harder than expected. A close alternative is 'walk in the park,' which is slightly more common in American speech. A natural reply is 'Tell me about it, I'm exhausted.'

distinctions.note: 'Walk in the park' and 'stroll in the park' mean the same thing, but 'walk in the park' is more common in American speech.
'Piece of cake' is an informal phrase for something easy, usually said with less emphasis on the hard work that came before.

collocations: not a stroll in the park
stroll in the park for me
hardly a stroll in the park

examples.everyday: Fixing the bike chain was no stroll in the park, but we got it done before dark.
examples.professional: Migrating the database was no stroll in the park, so plan for a full week of testing before the cutover.
examples.analytical: Teaching statistics to undergraduates is rarely a stroll in the park, since the concepts resist intuition and invite misreading.

nuance.analogy: It is like a path that looks flat on a map but turns out to be steep and rocky when you actually walk it.
nuance.etymology: 'Stroll' comes from German strolchen, and 'park' from Old French parc, enclosed land.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase to mean a literal stroll in a park, rather than something easy.
Saying 'stroll in a park' with 'a' instead of 'the' when referring to the idiom.

senses.definition: One who strolls.
senses.example: The stroller wandered along the river path, pausing now and then to watch the ducks.

senses.definition: A vagrant.
senses.example: The sheriff warned the stroller to leave town before sunset or face arrest.

senses.definition: Men's semiformal daytime dress comprising a gray or black single- or double-breasted coat, gray striped or checked formal trousers, a gray or silver necktie, and a gray, black or buff waistcoat.
senses.example: For the garden wedding, he chose a gray stroller with a silver necktie and matching waistcoat.

core.definition: A small wheeled seat or carriage that a parent pushes to carry a baby or young child.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final '-er' is a reduced rhotic vowel. Do not pronounce the final syllable as a full 'ah' or 'ayr'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for baby gear.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'stroller' is the everyday word for the wheeled seat you push a baby in, and parents use it constantly. British speakers say 'pushchair' or 'pram' for this, so you should use 'stroller' in an American store or with an American friend. The older word 'baby carriage' sounds dated, and 'stroller' also has a rare literary sense of someone who strolls, which Americans seldom use in conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Pram' is a British word for a baby carriage, so Americans would not normally use it; 'stroller' is the American equivalent.
A 'baby walker' is a frame that a baby stands in and moves around in, while a 'stroller' is a seat that is pushed by an adult.
'Baby carriage' is an older American term that sounds dated; 'stroller' is the modern and common word.

examples.everyday: Can you help me fold the stroller? The trunk is already full of groceries.
examples.professional: The daycare requires that every stroller be stored in the cubby area, so please label yours with your child's name.
examples.analytical: Urban planners measure sidewalk width against stroller clearance, since a double stroller needs far more space than a single pedestrian.

nuance.analogy: A stroller is like a small mobile seat that gives a baby a front-row view of the world as a parent walks.
nuance.etymology: From the verb stroll plus the agent suffix -er, used for the carriage that a person pushes for a child.
common_mistakes: Using 'pram' or 'pushchair' in American conversation, which sounds British.
Confusing a 'stroller' with a 'baby walker', which is a different device that the baby moves in.

senses.definition: A characteristic or ability at which one particularly excels.
senses.example: Patience is my strong point, so I usually handle difficult customers well.

core.definition: Something you are especially good at; a skill or quality that stands out as your best.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on POINT, and strong is lighter but still has a secondary stress. The words link smoothly, so the phrase sounds almost like 'strawng POINT' with the t lightly released.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it names a skill or quality you excel at.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in job interviews, performance reviews and friendly conversation. 'What are your strong points?' is a common interview question, and a natural reply is 'I'd say my strong point is X' or 'I'm strongest at X.' In casual talk, 'Cooking is my strong point' sounds natural and modest.

distinctions.note: Strength is the general quality or capacity, while a strong point is one specific thing you do well.
Forte is more formal and borrowed from French, so it sounds more polished or literary than the everyday strong point.
Strong suit is more casual and often used with 'not' to decline a task, while strong point is a more general term for a quality.

collocations: a strong point of the design

examples.everyday: Cooking is my strong point, so I'll make dinner tonight.
examples.professional: Clear communication is her strong point, so she usually leads the client calls.
examples.analytical: Empirical rigor is the strong point of the paper, though its theoretical framing is thin.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess player's favorite opening: the line you know you can play with confidence.
nuance.etymology: Strong from Old English strang; point from Latin punctum, meaning a pricking or dot.
common_mistakes: Saying 'my strong point in cooking' as a general phrase; 'my strong point is cooking' is more natural.
Using 'strong point' to mean physical strength of a building or object; it means a skill or quality.

senses.definition: A place built to withstand attack; a fortress.
A place of domination by, or refuge or survival of, a particular group or idea.
senses.example: the last stronghold of the Cornish language

core.definition: A fortified place built to resist attack; also a place where a group or idea is firmly entrenched and hard to dislodge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the word is a compound with a secondary stress on hold. Don't add a vowel between the ng and the h, and pronounce the final d clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in military or history contexts; negative when describing a group's entrenched power or a bad habit, and positive when describing a refuge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stronghold for a fortress in history or war, and figuratively for a place where a party, company or belief stays dominant, such as a city that is a political stronghold. In everyday talk you might say my dad's recliner is his stronghold. It is slightly literary, but common in news and sermons.

distinctions.note: A fortress is specifically a military building, while a stronghold can be any fortified place or a figurative base of power.
A refuge is a shelter from danger, whereas a stronghold can also be an aggressive base of power that resists outside control.

examples.everyday: My grandpa's recliner is his stronghold on Sunday afternoons, and nobody dares sit in it.
examples.professional: Our legacy billing system is still a stronghold for the finance team, so we can't retire it this quarter.
examples.analytical: Paul describes the arguments that resist the knowledge of God as strongholds that must be torn down, not merely debated.

nuance.analogy: A stronghold is like a castle on a hill: strong walls protect what is inside, and it is hard to take.
nuance.etymology: From strong plus hold, meaning a fortified place that can hold out against attack.
common_mistakes: Saying strongholt or stronghole, which mixes up the final sound; it ends in a clear d.
Using stronghold only for physical forts when Americans often use it figuratively for political or social bases.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is metsudah or matsod, meaning a fortress or stronghold, and the Greek is ochyroma, meaning a fortified place. Psalm 18:2 calls the LORD David's fortress and stronghold, a place of safety. Psalm 144:2 describes God as the one who is my stronghold and my fortress. Second Corinthians 10:4 speaks of divine weapons able to destroy strongholds, meaning proud arguments that oppose the knowledge of God.

senses.definition: A material with binder and aggregate that is used to coat interior walls or to make interior mouldings.
senses.example: The house's pale exterior stucco cracked after years of heavy rain.

senses.definition: A material with binder and aggregate that is used to coat exterior walls or to make exterior mouldings.
senses.example: The house's pale exterior stucco cracked after years of heavy rain.

senses.definition: A work made of stucco; stuccowork.
senses.example: The cathedral's ceiling features elaborate stucco that dates back to the seventeenth century.

senses.definition: To coat or decorate with stucco.
senses.example: They stuccoed the back wall to protect the bricks from moisture.

core.definition: A cement-like plaster used to coat outside walls, often textured, to give a finished look.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a short u as in cup, not oo. The final o is a clear oh sound, and the double c is pronounced as a k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a building material. Stucco is associated with Southwestern, Spanish, and Mediterranean-style houses, which many people find attractive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stucco in home building, real estate, and everyday talk about houses, especially in Florida, Texas, Arizona, and California. Interior plaster is usually called plaster or wall texture rather than stucco. Homeowners often discuss cracked stucco or stucco repairs in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Plaster is a general term for any wall coating, while stucco specifically means a cement-based coating used mainly on exteriors.
Drywall is a prefabricated board for interior walls, not a coating applied wet, so it is not stucco.

examples.everyday: Our new house has a pale stucco exterior that looks great in the sunshine.
examples.professional: The inspector found cracks in the stucco, so we need to schedule repairs before winter.
examples.analytical: The architect used stucco on the facade to echo the Mediterranean building traditions of the region.

nuance.analogy: Stucco is like a thick, hard coat of frosting that covers the outside of a house and protects the wall beneath.
nuance.etymology: From Italian stucco, meaning plaster or stucco, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Saying STOO-koh with a long oo vowel; the first vowel is short, like cup.
Using stucco for any wall plaster; in American usage it usually means the exterior coating.

stucco.etymology: Italian *stucco* (“coating made of pulverised gypsum, plaster, stucco”) from *stucco*, from *stucki* (“crust, fragment, piece”) from Proto-Germanic **stukkiją* (“stump, piece”), from Proto-Indo-European **tewg-* (“to shock, butt, impact”).

senses.definition: Situated beneath the Moon.
Of this world; earthly.

core.definition: Relating to the earthly realm beneath the moon, as opposed to the heavens; by extension, earthly, material and transient.

pronunciation.tip: The final syllable is a weak American 'er', and the word has three syllables, not four.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in cosmology, though in theology and literature it can suggest worldly and impermanent, often with mild negativity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use sublunar outside medieval and early modern cosmology, philosophy, theology, and literary writing. In everyday speech they say 'earthly', 'worldly' or 'material'. The more common form in English is sublunary, which means the same thing.

distinctions.note: The two words are synonyms, but sublunary is more common in English writing.
Earthly is common in everyday talk and can be neutral, while sublunar is a technical or literary term tied to ancient cosmology.
Worldly often suggests focus on wealth or status, while sublunar refers more broadly to the realm of change and decay below the heavens.

examples.everyday: After a long week, my friend said, Let's not stress about sublunar problems tonight.
examples.professional: The board discussion stayed on sublunar matters like headcount and budgets and never reached the long-term vision.
examples.analytical: Medieval cosmology separated the sublunar realm of change and decay from the unchanging heavens above.

nuance.analogy: Like the ground floor of a building compared with the roof, where everything below is changing and the heavens above are fixed.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sublunaris, from sub 'under' and luna 'moon'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in SUB-loo-ner, which is the stress pattern of the noun sublunary in some speakers but not in standard American speech.
Using sublunar in everyday conversation where earthly or material is more natural.
Assuming the word means literally under the moon in a physical sense only, when it also carries the moral and philosophical meaning of transience.

senses.definition: In a subservient manner.

core.definition: In a way that obeys others too readily, or acts as though one is inferior to them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUR, the second syllable, and the middle vee is quick. The -ly ending is a light 'lee'. Do not stress the -ent or -ly syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a lack of dignity or independence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subserviently to criticize someone who acts too eagerly to please people in power, such as a worker bowing to a boss. It is a formal, somewhat literary word and rarely used in casual talk. Saying someone 'answered subserviently' sounds sharp and disapproving.

distinctions.note: Obediently simply means following orders; subserviently adds a sense of excessive submission and loss of dignity.
Politely is positive or neutral; subserviently is negative because it suggests servility.

examples.professional: A junior analyst should not respond subserviently to every request from leadership; she should push back when the data says otherwise.
examples.analytical: In medieval thought, reason was expected to act subserviently toward faith, yet many philosophers resisted that subordination.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog that rolls over at every command, hoping for a treat, rather than acting as an equal partner.
nuance.etymology: From subservient plus the adverb suffix -ly; subservient from Latin subservire, 'to serve under'.
common_mistakes: Confusing subserviently with subservient. Subservient is the adjective; subserviently is the adverb.
Using the word neutrally. It is almost always negative, so it can insult a colleague.

senses.definition: The condition of being a subset.

core.definition: In mathematics and logic, the relationship in which every element of one set also belongs to another set.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUB, with lighter secondary stress on set and hood. The final -hood is /hʊd/, like 'hood' in 'neighborhood', not 'hud'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subsethood almost only in mathematics, logic, fuzzy set theory and computer science. Most people say 'is a subset of' rather than using the noun form. In a technical meeting, 'the subsethood check' is clear, but in everyday talk it would sound unnatural.

distinctions.note: Subset is the common noun for the smaller set; subsethood is the abstract noun for the relationship between sets.
A superset is the larger set that contains another; subsethood describes being contained in it.

examples.everyday: My son asked what subsethood means, and I had to look it up before I could explain.
examples.professional: Before we merged the tables, we checked subsethood to confirm that every customer ID appears in the master list.
examples.analytical: Subsethood defines a partial order on sets, which is why inclusion-based reasoning rests on it in both classical and fuzzy logic.

nuance.analogy: Like one box fitting completely inside a larger box, with nothing from the small box sticking out.
nuance.etymology: From subset plus the suffix -hood, 'state or condition of being'.
common_mistakes: Using subsethood in everyday talk where 'is a subset of' is more natural.
Confusing subsethood with membership. An element belongs to a set; a set is a subset of another set.

senses.definition: To use in place of something else, with the same function.
senses.example: I had no shallots so I substituted onion.

senses.definition: To use X in place of Y.
senses.example: I had to substitute new parts for the old ones.

senses.definition: To use Y in place of X; to replace X with Y.
senses.example: I had to substitute old parts with the new ones.

senses.definition: To serve as a replacement (for someone or something).
senses.example: Coach asked the freshman to substitute for the injured captain during the second half.

senses.definition: To remove (a player) from the field of play and bring on another in his place.
senses.example: He was playing poorly and was substituted after twenty minutes

senses.definition: A replacement or stand-in for something that achieves a similar result or purpose.
senses.example: Margarine is a common substitute for butter in baking, though the texture differs.

senses.definition: A substitute teacher.
senses.example: The school sent a substitute teacher, who had never met our class before.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of substitute good.
A player who is available to replace another if the need arises, and who may or may not actually do so.
senses.example: The coach kept a substitute on the bench in case someone got injured.

senses.definition: (historical) One who enlists for military service in the place of a conscript.
senses.example: In 1863, a wealthy man could pay a substitute to fight in his place.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To use one thing in place of another, so that the new item does the same job.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable in both the verb and the noun, so say SUB-stih-toot, not sub-STIT-oot. The last syllable is toot with a long oo, and the middle vowel is a quick, reduced sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word carries no judgment, although calling something a substitute can suggest it is a second-best choice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use substitute constantly in cooking, shopping and at work, as in 'Can I substitute oat milk for the regular milk?' A substitute teacher covers a class when the regular teacher is absent, and people often shorten it to 'sub.' Be aware that 'sub' also means a submarine-style sandwich, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Replace is the broad word for swapping something out, often for a newer or better version; substitute stresses that the new item fills the same role for now.
Stand in for is informal and usually describes a person temporarily taking someone's place; substitute is neutral and works for objects and ideas too.
An alternative is one of several options you can choose freely; a substitute is used because the original is missing or unavailable.

examples.everyday: Do you mind if I substitute almond milk for the regular milk? I'm out of it.
examples.professional: We can substitute the new API for the deprecated endpoint once QA signs off this sprint.
examples.analytical: We cannot simply substitute a proxy variable for the causal quantity the model was built to estimate.

nuance.analogy: Like a backup quarterback taking the field when the starter is hurt: same role, different player.
nuance.etymology: From Latin substituere, 'to put in the place of,' from sub- 'under' plus statuere 'to set up.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'substitute Y with X' in careful writing; the standard pattern is 'substitute X for Y.'
Stressing the second syllable (sub-STIT-oot); the stress belongs on SUB.

substitute.etymology: From Middle English *substituten*, from Latin *substitutus*, past participle of *substituō*, from *sub-* (“under; beneath”) + *statuō* (“to put up; establish”).

senses.definition: Subterranean.

core.definition: Existing or situated under the ground, especially in a natural or hidden place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RAY, the third syllable. The middle vowels are reduced to schwa, and the -ous ending is a light 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly dramatic. It suggests a hidden or mysterious space below the ground, often in fiction or poetry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use subterraneous today; they normally say subterranean, underground, or below ground. You may meet it in older books, poetry, or fiction describing caves or hidden passages. In everyday or professional speech, choose underground or subterranean instead.

distinctions.note: Subterranean is the common form and is used both literally and figuratively; subterraneous is rarer and more old-fashioned.
Underground is the everyday American word and can also mean a secret movement; subterraneous is literary and purely about location.

examples.professional: The geology report noted a subterraneous stream that feeds the well, though the surface map does not show it.
examples.analytical: The poet uses the image of a subterraneous river to suggest the buried memories that flow beneath everyday speech.

nuance.analogy: Subterraneous is like an old lantern in a museum: it still works, but most people now use a flashlight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subterraneus, from sub (under) and terra (earth).
common_mistakes: Using subterraneous in everyday conversation where underground is far more natural.
Confusing it with subterranean, which is the form Americans usually say and write.

senses.definition: The process of subtracting a number from another.
A calculation involving subtracting.
senses.example: The teacher has set us ten subtractions to do by tomorrow.

senses.definition: The removal of something.
senses.example: The subtraction of the wealth from the economy will result in recession.

core.definition: The arithmetic operation of taking one number away from another to find the difference, shown with the minus sign.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TRAK, and the vowel in the first syllable is a weak schwa. The t before r is a clear t, not a flap, so say the word as 'sub-TRAK-shun' with a hard k sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain technical term used in math, school, and everyday talk about counting or budgeting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subtraction for the math operation and often say 'take away' or 'minus' in casual speech. Teachers often call borrowing 'regrouping' in American elementary schools. In everyday talk you might say 'subtract five from twelve' rather than discuss the noun itself.

distinctions.note: Deduction usually means an amount taken off a total, such as a tax or payroll deduction, while subtraction is the arithmetic operation itself.
Minus is the sign or preposition used in subtraction, as in 'ten minus three', while subtraction is the name of the process.

examples.everyday: Can you help my son with his subtraction homework tonight?
examples.professional: The spreadsheet had a subtraction error that made our monthly revenue look lower than it was.
examples.analytical: Subtraction is not commutative, so five minus three and three minus five give different results.

nuance.analogy: Subtraction is like removing blocks from a tower and counting what is left.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subtrahere, 'to draw away from below,' from sub- 'under' plus trahere 'to draw.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'subtract to' instead of 'subtract from', as in 'subtract five from ten'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'sub-trac-TION' instead of 'sub-TRAC-tion'.

senses.definition: To perform two incompatible actions; to hold views which are in contradiction.
senses.example: He wants lower taxes and bigger budgets, which means he wants to suck and blow at once.

core.definition: To try to do or claim two things that contradict each other, so that you cannot succeed or be consistent.

pronunciation.tip: The word and is reduced to uhnd, and the main stress falls on blow. Keep the speech smooth so it sounds like one phrase.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The idiom criticizes someone for being inconsistent or for trying to have it both ways.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in arguments, workplace disagreements, and political talk to point out contradictory positions. It is less common than have it both ways, but people understand both. A natural reply is Yeah, you can't have it both ways.

distinctions.note: Have it both ways is more common in everyday speech. Suck and blow is more vivid and slightly more critical.
Contradict yourself describes saying two incompatible things. Suck and blow often describes wanting two incompatible outcomes.

collocations: trying to suck and blow at once
suck and blow on the same issue

examples.everyday: You can't complain about the noise and also want the party to go all night; you're trying to suck and blow.
examples.professional: We can't promise a fixed deadline and unlimited scope at the same time; that is sucking and blowing.
examples.analytical: The argument sucks and blows, affirming individual freedom while denying the choices that follow from it.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who breathes in and out at the same moment, trying to do two incompatible things with one action.
common_mistakes: Taking the idiom literally, as if it refers to physical sucking and blowing.
Changing the fixed word order, for example saying blow and suck.

senses.definition: The element symbolically associated with hellfire or damnation, or in alchemy, the fiery principle present in all things.
A yellowish green color, like that of sulfur.
senses.example: sulfur:

senses.definition: Any of various pierid butterflies of the subfamily Coliadinae, especially the sulfur-colored species.
A chemical element with atomic number 16, having a bright yellow color and characteristic smell, used commercially in a variety of products such as insecticides, black powder, and matchsticks.
Of a yellowish green color, like that of sulfur.
Having a characteristic sulfur-like smell, reminiscent of rotten eggs.
To treat with sulfur, or a sulfur compound, especially to preserve or to counter agricultural pests.

core.definition: A pale yellow nonmetal chemical element with a strong smell when burned, used in matches, fertilizers, and rubber.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SUL, and the final syllable is a reduced American r-colored 'er.' Many learners pronounce it with a separate 'ph' sound or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science and industry; in religious or literary settings it can carry a dark, fearful sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell it sulfur, not sulphur, which is the British spelling. In everyday speech, people might talk about the rotten-egg smell of sulfur, or the sulfur in matches. In Bible readings, the word is often translated brimstone, a term with strong associations with judgment and fire.

distinctions.note: Brimstone is an older English word for sulfur, used mainly in Bible translations and in sermons about hellfire.
Sulfurous describes something containing or smelling of sulfur, while sulfur is the element itself.

examples.everyday: The matches in that old box smell strongly of sulfur when you strike them.
examples.professional: We need to lower the sulfur content in the diesel to meet the new emissions standard.
examples.analytical: In older theological writing, sulfur was often linked symbolically with the fires of judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like the sharp smell that fills the air when a match is struck, a warning sign that something dangerous is burning.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sulfur, of uncertain origin, possibly from an earlier Indo-European root meaning 'to burn.'
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling sulphur in American writing.
Stressing the second syllable or adding an extra 'ph' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word gophrit, meaning sulfur or brimstone, appears in Genesis 19:24, where the LORD rains brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah. The Greek word theion, meaning sulfur, is used in the Book of Revelation for the fiery plagues and judgment. Revelation 14:10 and 21:8 describe the lake of fire, where the RSV uses the word brimstone to describe the torment of the wicked.

sulfur.etymology: From Middle English *sulphur*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *sulfre*, from Latin *sulfur*, from *sulpur* itself of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: A religious service on Easter practiced by some Protestant churches, usually observed in an outdoor setting.
senses.example: Our church holds a sunrise service on Easter morning in the park by the lake.

core.definition: A worship service held at sunrise, especially on Easter morning, often outdoors.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed in the compound: SUN-rise has the main stress on SUN, and SER-vice has the main stress on the first syllable. Americans also flap the t-like sound in 'service' only in fast speech, but here the sound is a clear s.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent. It suggests joy, hope, and a sense of community at the start of a holy day.
nuance.usage_note: Americans, especially in Protestant churches, use this phrase for an early Easter morning worship service, often held outdoors at a park, beach, or hilltop, sometimes followed by breakfast. Churches may post it as 'Sunrise Service, 6:30 a.m.' Saying it casually to a neighbor is natural in spring. A typical reply is 'Are you going?' or 'We'll be there, see you at the hill.'

distinctions.note: The Easter Vigil is a Roman Catholic service held on Holy Saturday night, while a sunrise service is usually held early Easter morning and is more typical of Protestant churches.
An Easter service is any Easter worship gathering, while a sunrise service specifically happens at dawn, often outdoors.

examples.everyday: Are you coming to the sunrise service on Sunday? We're meeting at the park at six.
examples.professional: The church staff is planning the sunrise service, so we need to confirm the volunteers and the sound equipment by Thursday.
examples.analytical: The sunrise service links the resurrection to the image of dawn, which the Gospels describe as the time the women came to the tomb.

nuance.analogy: A sunrise service is like a welcome party for the morning of Easter: people gather at the first light to celebrate the new day.
nuance.etymology: A compound of sunrise and service; sunrise from Old English sunne and rīsan, and service from Latin servitium through Old French.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress only on the first word, as 'sunrise service' with no stress on service; both words carry stress.
Calling it a sunrise mass, which is a Catholic term not used in most Protestant churches.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase is not a biblical term, but it draws on Easter accounts in which the women come to the tomb early in the morning. Mark 16:2 in the RSV says they came to the tomb when the sun had risen. John 20:1 says Mary Magdalene came early on the first day of the week while it was still dark. The custom links the resurrection to the image of dawn and the new day.

traditions.view: Orthodox churches celebrate Pascha with a midnight or late-night Paschal Vigil, where the light of the Resurrection is proclaimed in darkness. Dawn services are less central, though some parishes hold early morning gatherings.

Roman Catholics celebrate the Easter Vigil on Holy Saturday night, with the lighting of the Paschal candle and the Easter Mass. Some parishes also hold early morning Easter Masses, but a sunrise service is not the standard form of the liturgy.

Many Protestant churches, especially Baptist, Methodist, and nondenominational congregations, hold outdoor sunrise services on Easter morning. Lutheran and Reformed churches are more varied, and many use the sunrise service as a gathering for a shorter worship time.

senses.definition: Obsolete, antiquated.
senses.example: The superannuated software still ran on floppy disks, and nobody in the office knew how to fix it.

senses.definition: Retired or discarded due to age.

core.definition: Too old or out of date to be useful, or retired because of age.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third-syllable an, and the word has five syllables. Do not say 'AN-you-ay-ted' with a long o; the middle vowel is a quick yoo sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests something that is obsolete or a person who is past useful age, and it can sound unkind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use superannuated mainly in writing, especially in essays, editorials or literary criticism, and rarely in casual talk. In everyday speech they would say old, outdated or obsolete. Using it about a person can sound harsh, so it is best reserved for ideas, technology or systems.

distinctions.note: Obsolete means no longer in use because something newer has replaced it, and it is the more common everyday word.
Outdated is the neutral, everyday American term, while superannuated is more formal and often more disdainful.

examples.everyday: That old phone is totally superannuated, so you should upgrade it.
examples.professional: Our reporting dashboard is superannuated, so we plan to migrate it to a modern platform next quarter.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the author's model of the economy is superannuated, since it ignores the empirical evidence of the last fifty years.

nuance.analogy: Like a horse-drawn carriage on a highway, a superannuated idea still moves, but it no longer fits the road it is on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin super, beyond, and annus, year, via the sense of being beyond the usual age for work.
common_mistakes: Using superannuated in casual speech where outdated or old is more natural.
Confusing it with superannuation, which is a noun for a retirement pension in some contexts.

superannuated.etymology: From the Latin *superannuatus* (“more than one year old”), from *super* (“over”) (*super-*) + *annus* (“year”) (*annual*).

senses.definition: The state of being a survivor.
A right whereby a person becomes entitled to property by reason of his having survived another person who had an interest in it. It is one of the elements of a joint tenancy.
senses.example: Because the house was held in joint tenancy, survivorship passed it entirely to her brother.

senses.definition: The number or percentage of young that survive to adulthood.
senses.example: Researchers tracked the survivorship of tadpoles in the pond to measure how many reached adulthood.

core.definition: The state of surviving; in statistics and science, the proportion or rate of a group that stays alive or intact over a period of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VY, and the middle syllable is reduced to ur. The final -ship is short and light, with little stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science and law; it describes a measured rate or a legal right rather than an emotional state.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science, medicine, and biology, survivorship usually refers to the rate at which individuals or units stay alive or in a study, and survivorship bias is a common phrase. In American law, the term appears in joint tenancy with right of survivorship, a common way married couples hold property. It is not used in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Survival is the general state of staying alive, while survivorship in science often means a measured rate or proportion over time.
A survivor is a person, while survivorship describes the condition of a group or the rate at which members survive.

collocations: joint tenancy with right of survivorship

examples.everyday: Our house is in both our names with right of survivorship, so it goes to the other one of us if either of us dies.
examples.professional: The model was trained only on companies still in the database, so we introduced survivorship bias into the results.
examples.analytical: Survivorship in the observed sample can make failed strategies invisible, which is why sound inference must account for the missing cases.

nuance.analogy: Survivorship bias is like judging a plane's armor only by the planes that returned from battle, forgetting the ones that were shot down.
nuance.etymology: From survivor, from survive, with the suffix -ship denoting a state or condition.
common_mistakes: Using survivorship to mean a person; say survivor for a person.
Forgetting survivorship bias, which means assuming that a sample of survivors represents the whole population, including those who did not survive.

senses.definition: Capable of being swallowed (physically).
senses.example: Some medical techniques monitor the inside of the body by means of a swallowable miniature camera.

senses.definition: Relatively easy to swallow.
Able to be accepted by the electorate.

core.definition: Able to be swallowed, or, figuratively, easy enough to accept, especially a pill or an unpleasant idea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SWAH, and reduce the ending -able to a weak 'uh-buhl'. Do not turn it into 'swal-AY-bul'; the stress stays on the root.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing medicine; figuratively it suggests a compromise people can accept.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use swallowable mostly about pills, capsules or food textures, and occasionally about proposals people can accept. In everyday speech they more often say easy to swallow or easy to take. Calling a plan swallowable can sound stiff or like polished news language. A natural reply to a hard-to-accept plan is 'Yes, the new policy is easier to swallow now.'

distinctions.note: Easy to swallow is the everyday American idiom; swallowable is more formal and much less common.
Acceptable describes something adequate; swallowable often suggests something bitter that people can tolerate.

examples.everyday: The new children's medicine comes in a small, swallowable tablet, which is a relief for my kids.
examples.professional: The pharmacy team wants the pill redesigned so it is swallowable for older patients.
examples.analytical: A policy becomes swallowable only after it has been sweetened, and the honest question is whose interests the sweetening serves.

nuance.analogy: Like a pill with a sugar coating: the same bitter substance, now easier to take.
nuance.etymology: From swallow (Old English swelgan) plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Moving the stress onto the suffix, as in 'swallow-AY-ble'; the stress stays on swallow.
Using swallowable in casual speech where easy to swallow sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Something used to swat with; a flyswatter.
Someone who swats.
senses.example: Our cabin's loudest swatter spent every July evening chasing mosquitoes around the porch.

core.definition: A tool, usually a flat plastic mesh on a handle, used to swat flies and other insects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SWAH. The middle t is a flap, like the d in ladder, and the final -er is a quick, reduced vowel rather than a full syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes a household tool with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say fly swatter for the household tool, and often shorten it to swatter when the context is clear. The sense of a person who swats is rare outside sports or informal writing. A typical request at home is Can you hand me the fly swatter?

distinctions.note: Fly swatter is the full, most natural form for the household tool; swatter alone is shorter and works when context is clear.
Bug spray kills insects with a chemical from a distance; a swatter is a physical tool used by hand.

examples.everyday: Hand me the fly swatter, there's a wasp by the window.
examples.professional: Facilities ordered new swatters for the break room after the fruit flies came back.
examples.analytical: The humble fly swatter illustrates how simple tools can solve local problems without addressing the conditions that breed pests.

nuance.analogy: A fly swatter is like a tiny tennis racket for insects: a flat surface that meets a quick, targeted hit.
nuance.etymology: From swat (to hit sharply) plus the agent suffix -er, one who or that which swats.
common_mistakes: Saying fly hitter or fly killer instead of fly swatter, the standard American term.
Pronouncing the final -er as a full syllable like air; it is a reduced, unstressed vowel.

senses.definition: Swim away from the shore toward something.

core.definition: To swim away from the shore toward open water or toward something in the distance.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OUT. Pronounce the vowel as a diphthong, like ow in cow, so it sounds like owt rather than oot.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Can sound alarming when a swimmer is far from shore or caught in a current.
nuance.usage_note: Lifeguards and parents use it, as in Don't swim out past the buoys. Add to and a destination to name the target, as in swim out to the raft. Without a destination, it simply means moving away from shore.

distinctions.note: Swim away suggests leaving or escaping; swim out describes moving from the shore toward open water.
Swim across means crossing from one side to the other, not moving away from the shore.

examples.everyday: Don't swim out too far, the water is cold today.
examples.professional: The safety team asked staff to remind guests not to swim out beyond the marked area.
examples.analytical: A swimmer who swims out into open water relies on judgment as much as strength, because the shore can grow distant quickly.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat leaving the dock, you move steadily away from the safe place.
nuance.etymology: Swim from Old English swimman; out from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the destination in the phrase swim out to, as in swim out to the dock
Using swim out with a direct object as if it were transitive

conversation.text: Don't swim out past the buoys.
Let's swim out to the raft and back.
He swam out too far, and the lifeguard blew the whistle.

senses.definition: A relationship of mutual benefit, especially among different species.
The close and long-term relationship or interaction between two or more different species.
senses.example: Bees and flowers display symbiosis. The bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated.

senses.definition: The close and long-term relationship or interaction between two or more different species in which all organisms benefit; mutualism.
senses.example: Bees and flowers display symbiosis. The bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated.

senses.definition: The state of people of different types, races, cultures, communities, etc. living together.
senses.example: The town's symbiosis of Lebanese and Polish families produced a shared bakery and festival.

senses.definition: The occurrence of two different or opposing things in the same time and place.
senses.example: The film's symbiosis of despair and humor made it both painful and oddly uplifting.

core.definition: A close, long-term relationship between two different species, often in which both organisms benefit.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the "oh" syllable, the third. The "-bi-" is pronounced "bye", not "bee". The final "-sis" is a weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in biology; it can be used positively for a partnership that helps both sides.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use symbiosis in biology, ecology and science writing. In general conversation it can describe a close and mutually helpful relationship between people or companies, but it sounds more formal than "partnership". The adjective symbiotic is more common in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Mutualism is one type of symbiosis in which both species benefit. Symbiosis is the broader term for any close, long-term relationship between species.
Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship in which one species benefits at the expense of the other. Symbiosis itself does not require either side to benefit.

examples.everyday: My friend says the two of them have a kind of symbiosis, since she handles the money and he handles the cooking.
examples.professional: The partnership with the vendor is a real symbiosis, since each team gets what it needs from the other.
examples.analytical: Lichens illustrate symbiosis, where a fungus and an alga live together in a relationship that neither could sustain alone.

nuance.analogy: Symbiosis is like a rowing team in which each person pulls the boat forward and depends on the others to keep it steady.
nuance.etymology: From Greek symbiōsis, "living together", from syn- "together" and bios "life".
common_mistakes: Assuming symbiosis always means both sides benefit, when the term can also describe parasitism.
Using the noun in place of the adjective, as in "a symbiosis relationship" instead of "a symbiotic relationship".

senses.definition: A character or glyph representing an idea, concept or object.
senses.example: "$" is the symbol for dollars in the US and some other countries.

senses.definition: A thing considered the embodiment or cardinal exemplar of a concept, theme, or other thing.
senses.example: The lion is the symbol of courage; the lamb is the symbol of meekness or patience.

senses.definition: A type of noun whereby the form refers to the same entity independently of the context; a symbol arbitrarily denotes a referent. See also icon and index.
senses.example: My linguistics professor argued that the English word 'dog' is a symbol, not an icon.

senses.definition: A summary of a dogmatic statement of faith.
senses.example: The Apostles, Nicene Creed and the confessional books of Protestantism, such as the Augsburg Confession of Lutheranism are considered symbols.

senses.definition: The numerical expression which defines a plane's position relative to the assumed axes.
senses.example: The engineer entered the plane's symbol into the coordinate table before running the transform.

senses.definition: An internal identifier used by a debugger to relate parts of the compiled program to the corresponding names in the source code.
senses.example: The debugger loaded the symbol table so I could see variable names instead of memory addresses.

senses.definition: A signaling event on a communications channel; a signal that cannot be further divided into meaningful information.
senses.example: Each symbol on the serial line carried three bits, so the receiver decoded it at once.

senses.definition: To symbolize.
senses.example: The dove was chosen to symbol peace in the church's stained glass windows.

core.definition: A mark, object or image that stands for an idea, quality or thing, such as a flag standing for a nation or a dove standing for peace.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced and the l is syllabic, so the word sounds like 'SIM-buhl', not 'sim-bowl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, depending on context. A symbol can be inspiring, like a flag, or negative, like a status symbol that suggests showing off.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use symbol constantly for flags, logos, national emblems and objects that carry meaning, as in 'a symbol of hope'. In mathematics and chemistry it means a letter or notation, such as pi or Fe, so context matters. Use 'symbol of' rather than 'symbol for' when talking about ideas.

distinctions.note: A sign points to something by natural connection or practical information, such as smoke suggesting fire, while a symbol stands for something by cultural or conventional meaning.
An emblem is a fixed, official design used to identify a group or organization, such as a coat of arms, while a symbol can be any object or image with a meaning.
An icon resembles what it depicts, like a portrait or a computer-screen picture of a printer, while a symbol's link to its meaning is often arbitrary or cultural.

examples.everyday: The eagle on the flag is a symbol of American freedom, or so my kids keep telling me.
examples.professional: In the dashboard, the red icon is the symbol for a failed job, so please don't change its color without telling the team.
examples.analytical: The cross is a symbol whose meaning depends on the community that reads it, so its significance cannot be fixed by its shape alone.

nuance.analogy: A symbol is like a name tag: it stands in for the person or idea without being that person or idea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin symbolum, from Greek sumbolon, 'token' or 'sign', from symballein 'to throw together'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'symbol for peace' when 'symbol of peace' sounds more natural for an idea.
Pronouncing the second syllable fully as 'bol' instead of the reduced 'buhl'.

symbol.etymology: From French *symbole*, from Latin *symbolus*, *symbolum* (“a sign, mark, token, symbol, in Late Latin also a creed”), from Ancient Greek *σύμβολον* (“a sign by which one infers something; a mark, token, badge, ticket, tally, check, a signal, watchword,…

senses.definition: The junction between the terminal of a neuron and either another neuron or a muscle or gland cell, over which nerve impulses pass.
senses.example: Dopamine crosses the synapse to signal the next neuron in the circuit.

senses.definition: To form a synapse.
senses.example: Neurons in the developing cortex begin to synapse with their targets within weeks.

senses.definition: To undergo synapsis.
